title: The Round-Middle Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra
author: Annotated by Master Dayou; commentated by Master Chuandeng (translated)
excerpt: Taking the retribution-body and the environment of the Land of Bliss as the wonderful being of the one-mind, and the invoking of the name as true emptiness: without true emptiness one cannot realize the wonderful being of the Land of Bliss, and without wonderful being one cannot reveal the true emptiness of this mind.

blocks.text: Preface to the Round-Middle Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra

inline.s: The Tathagata's secret speech lies in words whose meaning is manifold. It is like a king who asked for the saindhava: a single name embracing four real things. Only that wise minister understood its meaning—whether the king was about to go out, to eat, to drink, or to go to war, as soon as he uttered that one word, the minister presented him with a horse, with salt, with water, or with a vessel, never failing to grasp the king's mind and to suit his intention. The wise minister, the bodhisattva, is likewise: he well understands whatever the Tathagata teaches, expounding the shallow deeply and the deep in a shallow way, declaring what is neither shallow nor deep within that which is both shallow and deep, and what is both shallow and deep within that which is neither shallow nor deep. In composing treatises and spreading the scriptures he makes the full and the brief each fit its place—neither causing wisdom to regress nor leaving the truth deficient. Only then may he be said to have ascended the hall and entered the inner chamber. Now this Amitābha Sutra is what Śākyamuni Tathagata set forth as a shallow explanation within the deep and a brief explanation within the vast. Since the exposition was brief, the wise minister's commentary upon it could not but be brief; since the meaning is deep, his commentary could not but be deep. The brief commentary does not cause wisdom to regress, and the profound principle does not leave the truth deficient. He reaches the vast by way of the brief and takes the middle way with composure. I have seen the Brief Explanation of Master Qu'an at Wumen. Its preface says: 'The bejeweled groves and the jade-like pools directly reveal the mind-source; the measure of longevity and the light fully manifest the self-nature.' Again it says: 'Realizing that which is originally complete within the mind, the countless lands are not far away; knowing that the great vows may be relied upon, the three asamkhya kalpas are crossed transversely.' Alas! It gathers the whole sutra into itself, and yet its words are so very brief; it concerns the mind-nature and the self-nature, and yet its meaning is so very deep. Were it not for the bodhisattva, the wise minister, how could anyone arrive at such a point? Now I make this commentary and have entitled it specifically 'Round-Middle.' The intent is this: taking the retribution-body and the environment of the Land of Bliss as the wonderful being of the one-mind, and the invoking of the name as true emptiness. Without true emptiness one cannot realize the wonderful being of the Land of Bliss, and without wonderful being one cannot reveal the true emptiness of this mind. This is what is called the 'inconceivable provisional'—not the one-sided provisional—and 'true emptiness not empty'—not mere emptiness. Uniting these two and practicing them, the Round-Middle is rounded and complete, and the path of the 'not-merely-middle' is accomplished. Therefore it is named a commentary. My wish is that those who read this sutra and practice it may, mindful of its name, think upon its meaning. Truly they should single-mindedly remain unconfused, forgetting all deliberations, and the principle of true emptiness will be manifest. Holding the name for seven days, thought after thought continuous, the principle of wonderful being will be revealed. When the practice is complete, one sees the Buddha; when the mind is pure, the lotus opens. When the seal of Sahā is broken, the text of the Land of Bliss is accomplished. The breaking of the seal is that by which feeling is emptied—this is called true emptiness; the accomplishment of the text is that by which the Dharma is established—this is called wonderful being. Both are forgotten and both are preserved. Hence the words of the Amitābha Sutra are brief and its meaning is deep. Because this commentary follows in order, I here set forth the meaning of the title, and so I write this informal preface.
Written at the time of the newly brightened moon in the last month of winter, in the first year of the dragon's ascent to the throne of the Great Ming under the Tianqi reign. Hence this preface.

blocks.text: Explaining the Preface
Preface to the Brief Explanation of the Amitābha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha

inline.s: By the monk Dayou of Wu Commandery, Ming dynasty.

blocks.text: Next, the person who composed it.

inline.s: The master's style was Qu'an, and Dayou was his given name. He was abbot of the Beichan Tiantai Teaching Temple in Suzhou, deeply versed in doctrinal principles, and in the Pure Land path he especially grasped its subtlety. He wrote a Pure Land Compendium (Jingtu Zhigui Ji), which is now widely current in the world. His lay surname and ancestral home still await detailed verification.

Third, the explanation of the preface, in two parts. First, the reason for expounding the sutra; second, the reason for the brief annotation. The first has two parts: first, the rise of the occasion; second, the exposition of the sutra. The first in turn has two: first, the tracing of the source-stream; second, the actual account of the occasion. And the first of these has two: first, the true source is non-dual; second, the delusive streams produce distinctions.

Now when the true source is taken up, then within the one nature there is originally no distinction of suffering and joy; why then should the Tathagata appear in the world and preach a sutra? It is only because the delusive streams have produced distinctions that our Buddha manifested birth to spread the teaching. So first we make clear that the true source is non-dual.
[Commentary] Now the Still-Light is truly pure; originally there is no distinction of suffering and joy.

[Sub-commentary] 'Still-Light' is one of the four kinds of Pure Land. The four Pure Lands are: first, the Pure Land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together; second, the Pure Land of Expedient Remainder; third, the Pure Land of Real Reward and Non-obstruction; and fourth, the Pure Land of Everlasting Still-Light. Each has its pure and its impure aspect, and only the highest grade of Still-Light is the true Pure Land; the remaining Pure Lands all carry a provisional element. One must further know that the expression 'truly pure' does not mean that apart from the three lands there is some separate Still-Light to be had; it merely points to the substance of the three lower lands, whose principle is fundamentally ultimate and no different from Still-Light. Hence the Venerable Siming, in the Miaozong Chao, says: 'Know that the four lands are both horizontal and vertical, and further know that the horizontal and the vertical are only in a single place. Take the land of cohabitation: place it in one spot, and it is at once the Real Reward. One who breaks through ignorance and turns to enter that is the Dharma-body, sharing the substance and function of the Buddha and called the true, marvelous reward—even a person with purified six faculties cannot take part in it, much less a two-vehicle practitioner. This is the vertical, an instance where in one place the Real Reward is discussed. Again, if one has not broken ignorance and sees it while still in this body, this is what the Buddhas and the great bodhisattvas, for the sake of those able to see, add, causing them to see the Real Reward land. For there are those whose capacities, though not yet free of delusion, have already practiced the middle contemplation; as in the Avatamsaka assembly and other gatherings, beings of sundry types all see an inconceivable body and land. Since the Real Reward is thus, Expedient and Still-Light, in their horizontal discussion in the same place, are likewise. In the place of cohabitation one discusses the horizontal and vertical of the three lands; in the place of Expedient, the horizontal and vertical of the two lands; in the place of Real Reward, the horizontal and vertical of the one land. But at Still-Light there is neither horizontal nor vertical—even in that very place there is none. Now to say 'the Still-Light is truly pure' is to mark the true substance directly. 'Originally there is no distinction of suffering and joy' reveals the transcendence of error and the negation of the false. For if the purity and impurity of the four lands are spoken of: in the Sahā of cohabitation there is only suffering and no joy, while in Qingtai there is only joy and no suffering. Comparing Expedient with cohabitation, cohabitation has only suffering and Expedient only joy. Taking Expedient in its own land, its impure region has only suffering and its pure region only joy. Comparing Real Reward with Expedient, Expedient has only suffering and Real Reward only joy. Taking Real Reward in its own land, its impure region has only suffering and its pure region only joy. Comparing Real Reward with Still-Light, Real Reward has only suffering and Still-Light only joy. Taking Still-Light in its own land, its impure region has only suffering and its pure region only joy. All of the foregoing is spoken in terms of what is accomplished through cultivation—non-dual yet dual—and so there is the distinction of suffering and joy. But the preface's words 'originally there is no distinction of suffering and joy' refer to the nature endowed with the ten realms: those aggregates and lands have only the fused nature of the suffering and joy of the ten realms, and not the differentiated characteristics of the suffering and joy of the ten realms. That is, the unchanging suchness equally possessed by living beings and Buddhas, which originally has no distinction of purity and impurity—how could there be a difference of suffering and joy? Hence this single phrase is sectioned as 'the true source is non-dual,' serving as the basis for the following 'delusive streams produce distinctions.' This is what the Surangama Sutra calls 'the nature-consciousness is subtle and bright, the original consciousness is bright and subtle,' and again, 'pure and of itself so, pervading the dharma-realm.' The four kinds of Pure Land are given in full below.

blocks.text: Next, delusive streams produce distinctions.

inline.s: [Commentary] Delusive consciousness, in its teeming confusion, then brings about the difference of sages and ordinary beings.

[Sub-commentary] 'Delusive consciousness' is the collective name for the three delusions. For living beings, from beginningless time, within the subtle brightness of the nature-consciousness and the bright subtlety of the original consciousness, a single thought suddenly darkened, and falsely made a shining awareness. Because of awareness a locus was set up; the locus having been falsely set, false capacity arose. Within the undifferentiated, blazingly it became differentiated, serving as the three subtle marks; and then ignorance and dust-like delusion served as the six coarse marks. The views and thoughts, in the first transformation, became the impure Still-Light; in the second, the impure Real Reward; in the third, the impure Expedient; in the fourth, the impure cohabitation. Thus they became bodhisattvas, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, and beings of the six realms. Hence it is said, 'Delusive consciousness in its teeming confusion then brings about the difference of sages and ordinary beings.' This is what the Surangama Sutra calls 'following the minds of beings, as their measuring capacity'; and what the Avatamsaka Sutra means by 'able to follow the conditions of purity and defilement, thereby dividing the ten dharma-realms.' For this reason it is sectioned as 'delusive streams produce distinctions.' One must further understand that though the first line says 'the Still-Light is truly pure, originally free of the distinction of suffering and joy,' it does not preclude non-distinction yet distinction—that is, the nature endowed with the ten realms. And though the second line says 'delusive consciousness in its teeming confusion then brings about the difference of sages and ordinary beings,' it does not preclude distinction yet non-distinction—that is, that within the nature there is no difference. This is precisely because, though suchness is unchanging, it does not preclude its changing yet following conditions; and though delusive consciousness follows conditions, it does not preclude its following conditions yet remaining unchanging. Because of the conditions of conditions, therefore, there is non-distinction yet distinction; because of the unchanging, there is distinction yet non-distinction. One who can understand this is able to grasp that this thought of Buddha-recitation is the whole nature arising to bring about pure practice, and the whole practice being gathered within the one nature.

blocks.text: Next, the actual account of the rise of the occasion.

inline.s: [Commentary] Therefore, drifting through the five turbidities and unable to return to the one true, our Śākyamuni manifested birth in the world of endurance.

[Sub-commentary] This is the actual account of the rise of the occasion for the Tathagata's preaching of the sutra. The Tathagata had long realized the true and constant, so why should he have been born into a king's palace? It was solely because all living beings, from beginningless time, had fallen, that there was this appearing in the Sahā world. 'Drifting through the five turbidities' means that living beings, from beginningless time, from the ocean of the nirvāṇa nature roused the waves of consciousness, obscuring the perfect clarity and losing the serene depth, muddying the bright subtlety and drowning the true nature. This is because first they lost it through movement—hence 'drifting.' This is what the Surangama Sutra means by 'the bright awareness and the empty darkness, mutually dependent, give rise to agitation.' Next they lost it through dullness—hence the 'five turbidities,' which the Surangama Sutra calls 'darkness obscured becoming emptiness.' Yet dullness must contain movement, and movement must contain dullness; thus drifting is turbidity, and turbidity is drifting. Once the delusion of dullness and movement has taken form, the truth of brightness and stillness is lost. Only these five turbidities differ as coarse and fine. As the Surangama Sutra says of the turbidity of the kalpa: 'You see empty space pervading the ten directions; space and sight are not separated. There is emptiness without a substance; there is sight without awareness. Woven together, falsehood is formed; this is the first, called the turbidity of the kalpa.' This speaks together of the three delusions. If, as the ordinary explanation has it, only when human life was twenty thousand years did one enter the turbidity of the kalpa, that singles out the two delusions of views and thoughts at their most blazing. And yet there may be the fine without the coarse, but never the coarse without the fine. Now this points directly to the time of Śākyamuni's manifest birth in the world of endurance, when the coarse suited the capacity. If it says 'unable to return to the one true,' that too speaks together with the fine. The manifestation of birth in the world of endurance is precisely the response of descending—the impure cohabitation land of ordinary beings and sages, spoken of merely as the humble response of a sixteen-foot aged monk's body and appearance. If the fine delusions are also included, the meaning embraces the response descending into the upper two lands.

blocks.text: Next, the exposition of the sutra is divided into two: first, the account of the place and the capacities; second, the account of the essential teaching. Now first, the account of the place and capacities.

inline.s: [Commentary] At the auspicious gathering in the Jeta Grove he addressed the sharp faculties of Shariputra.

[Sub-commentary] The auspicious gathering in the Jeta Grove is the place where the sutra was preached; Shariputra, of sharp faculties, is the one whose capacity was met. In discussing the capacities to which this sutra is addressed, there are three grades: first, bodhisattvas; second, the two vehicles; third, ordinary beings. For the Pure Land teaching the various lesser-vehicle sutras do not speak of at all, since once the fruits and the effects have been exhausted the body is extinguished and consciousness destroyed, and nothing is said of birth after death. Now this is spoken at length, and it is a bodhisattva teaching. If one traces its origin, the sutra was preached in the Vaipulya [Expanded] period, precisely at the time of refuting the one-sided and censuring the lesser, extolling the greater and extolling the Round. Censuring the lesser vehicles, who are not reborn outside the realms, it says 'there is birth,' and especially points to that land as having immeasurable, unbounded shravaka disciples; and it praises to the utmost the subtle, wonderful adornments of that land's retribution-body and environment. Thus the extolling of the greater and the extolling of the Round are lodged within it. Moreover, Sariputra was foremost among the many disciples, so he addressed him, causing him to turn from the lesser to the greater. As for the capacities directly aimed at, they are those in the ordinary state; holding the name for seven days with a single minded, unconfused heart, they immediately attain rebirth; and once they have entered that auspicious assembly they attain non-retrogression. Viewed thus, though these are ordinary beings, the teaching belongs to the Round and to the Sudden, as is also to be known.

blocks.text: Next, the essential teaching as explained, in four parts. First, the account of the sutra's name; second, the account of the sutra's substance; third, the account of its cardinal purport; fourth, the account of its function and power. The expression and the expressed lie within these four, so they are gathered and set forth in order to exhaust the purport of the whole sutra. One may well call him a person thoroughly versed in the Great Vehicle. Now first, the account of the sutra's name.

inline.s: [Commentary] He opens the vow-gate of the dharma-treasury and points to the wonderful land of the Land of Bliss.

[Sub-commentary] This sutra fully sets forth the retribution-body and the environment, together with the assemblies, and these are the expression that names it; yet the sutra-title says only 'The Buddha speaks of Amitābha.' As the Great Master's commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: 'Raise the proper retribution to gather in the dependent fruition, and describe the teaching lord to include the assemblies.' That is to say, the title speaks only of the proper, raising the proper to gather in the dependent; the preface speaks only of the dependent, raising the dependent to gather in the proper. This cross-reference is the craft of the composition. As for this sutra not expounding the opening of the vow-gate, it is because the Larger Sutra states it in detail, and so it is omitted here.

blocks.text: Next, the account of the sutra's substance.

inline.s: [Commentary] The bejeweled groves and the jade-like pools directly reveal the mind-source; the measure of longevity and the light fully manifest the self-nature.

[Sub-commentary] 'The bejeweled groves and jade-like pools' briefly raises the dependent retribution of which the sutra speaks, from the passage on the seven rows of railings down to the jeweled trees and jeweled nets emitting subtle sounds—one section of the scripture. 'The measure of longevity and the light' briefly raises the proper retribution of which it speaks, from the passage 'For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha' down to 'It can only be spoken of as immeasurable, unbounded asamkhyeyas'—another section. 'Directly reveal the mind-source; fully manifest the self-nature'—these two lines properly describe its substance. For this sutra takes the seal of reality as its proper substance: the formless yet all-formed, the formed yet formless, is called real-form. Now the bejeweled groves and jade-like pools, the measure of longevity and the light, are certainly the characteristics of all dharmas; yet if they directly reveal the mind-source and fully manifest the self-nature, what characteristic can be obtained? This is precisely the proper substance of the formless-yet-formed and the formed-yet-formless. The wonderful teaching of a Pure Land that is the mind and an Amitābha that is the self-nature is easy to utter but hard to make precise; one who would profoundly apprehend its purport must arrive at what is most fitting. If one seeks to clarify it, the Tiantai teaching of the dharma-nature alone suffices. Why? The Land of Bliss lies far beyond a hundred thousand ko?i of lands, and Amitābha Buddha is a person of fruit, complete in wisdom and severance and pure in fulfillment. An ordinary being of the ordinary ground, defiled by the three delusions and sunk in the two deaths, creating inexhaustible karma-entanglements and making never-ending causes of birth, how could he suddenly respond to Amitābha, be reborn in the Pure Land, cut across the five destinies, and at once reach non-retrogression? It is precisely because in this school's exposition the dharma-nature of living beings has three meanings. First, the nature's measure: it pervades the ten directions and interpenetrates with nothing outside—the Land of Bliss beyond a hundred thousand ko?i of lands is within our nature's measure only a close-adjacent corner. Second, the nature's substance: what is everlastingly constant and firmly set, pure and luminous—Amitābha's wisdom and severance, the complete awakened substance—corresponds to our nature's substance ultimately and without difference. Third, the nature's endowment: but if one speaks only of 'nothing outside' and 'no difference' without understanding the gateway of the nature's endowment, then though one says 'nothing outside,' in the end there remains an outside, and though one says 'no difference,' in the end there remains a difference. Nor would one know from what cause the virtue of the nature's measure and substance is pervasive, or by what means it is pure. Know that there is the endowment of the nature: then what was before called the virtue of substance and the virtue of measure all have the nature's endowment as their root. The purport of the three natures is fully set out in the Treatise on Birth and Non-birth, and is not enumerated at length here.

blocks.text: Third, the account of the cardinal purport.

inline.s: [Commentary] The assembly of many sages abide in one place; it is not by small virtue that one is reborn there. Holding the name for seven days lies in the single-mindedness that is unconfused.

[Sub-commentary] Hereafter, in the explanation of the title's five sections, faith, vows, and the pure karma are taken as the cardinal purport of the whole sutra. Now, gathering the scripture and giving a brief account, it speaks only of the pure karma, because among the three essentials this is the proper one. The first line corresponds to the scripture's 'That Buddha has immeasurable, unbounded shravaka disciples, all arhats, beyond the reach of calculation; the host of bodhisattvas are likewise.' Again it says, 'Of those reborn in the Land of Bliss, all are avivartika [non-retrogressing]; many among them are in a single lifetime destined to Buddhahood, their number impossible to calculate, and can only be spoken of as immeasurable, unbounded asamkhyeyas.' Again it says, 'Living beings who hear this should make the vow to be reborn in that land. Why? Because they may gather in one place with such hosts of superior good people.' The second line corresponds to the scripture's 'It cannot be by small roots of goodness and the causes and conditions of merit that one is reborn in that land.' Hence 'the assembly of many sages abide in one place; it is not by small virtue that one is reborn there.' The third and fourth lines correspond to the scripture's 'If there be good men and good women who hear of Amitābha Buddha and hold fast to his name, for one day, for two days, and up to seven days, single-minded and unconfused.' Precisely because the bejeweled groves and the jade-like pools directly reveal the mind-source, and the measure of longevity and the light fully manifest the self-nature, and because living beings from beginningless time, through the causes and conditions of dullness and movement, have drifted through the five turbidities and cannot return to the one true—now when they are about to return to the root and revert to the source, nothing precedes illuminating the dullness and stilling the movement. Holding the name for seven days is what illuminates its dullness; single-minded and unconfused is what stills its movement. When dullness and movement are both forgotten, what is there to await for the true? It is like dust cleared and the mirror bright, the wind quieted and the waves still. Yet that the mere holding of the name for seven days should at once reach non-retrogression shows precisely that the teaching belongs to the Round and the Sudden—that without waiting a single lifetime, the profound power of the vows, the compassion that gives and takes away, and the fundamental merit-power are inconceivable. This is truly the vital ford that quickly escapes birth-and-death and the highway of the bodhisattva's practice.

blocks.text: Fourth, the account of the function and power, in two parts. First, the proper statement of the function and power.

inline.s: [Commentary] Matters and principle are one in substance; living beings and the Buddha are originally the same. The compassion that is without conditions responds without forethought.

[Sub-commentary] This sutra takes the leaving of suffering and the attainment of joy as its function. That is, the scripture says: 'When that person's life comes to an end, Amitābha Buddha with the hosts of sages appear before him. When that person ends, his mind is not inverted, and he immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.' Thus the function and power of this sutra concern the giving and the taking away. The work of giving and taking away lies in the response and the sensing. Living beings, with single-minded holding of the name, form the sensing; Amitābha, with the taking away of suffering and the bestowal of joy, forms the response. The way of taking away suffering is grounded in compassion, and the way of bestowing joy is grounded in kindness; both are the natural relation of the essential nature, not in the least forced. The practitioner takes as his sensing the way that matters and principle are one in substance and living beings and the Buddha are fundamentally the same; Amitābha takes as his response the way that the unconditioned compassion responds without forethought. Is it not then that Amitābha, by coming without coming, comes to this Sahā to receive and guide the practitioner; and the practitioner, by going without going, goes to that Land of Bliss to behold and bow to Amitābha? This is truly the rational basis on which the function and power of this sutra rely.

blocks.text: Next, the merit and works that are brought forth.

inline.s: [Commentary] Realizing the originally complete in the mind, the countless lands are not far; knowing that the great vows may be relied upon, the three asamkhya kalpas are cut across transversely.

[Sub-commentary] The foregoing already made clear the rational basis of the function and power. Relying on it to invoke the Buddha and seek rebirth: one who can realize that matters and principle are one in substance and living beings and the Buddha are fundamentally the same, then the far region of the hundred thousand ko?i of lands is all the originally complete of my own mind—though far, it is not far. One who can know that the unconditioned compassion responds without forethought, then the forty-eight great vows are unconditionally reliable, and the stream of consciousness can be cut across. Such is the function and power—is it not surpassing? As for 'cutting across the three asamkhya kalpas': this shows that transcending the three realms has both a vertical and a horizontal sense. According to the Abhidharma, a bodhisattva of the Tripitaka through three asamkhya kalpas practices the six perfections and the myriad practices, plants for a hundred kalpas the cause of the marks of excellence, and then reaches non-retrogression and attains the fivefold dharma-body. This is the vertical exit, ascending from below to above, like a rabbit or a horse crossing a river in a winding, lengthy way. But those who, in accordance with this sutra, seek rebirth in the Land of Bliss—whether already reborn, currently reborn, or to be reborn—all attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Again it says, 'Those reborn there are all avivartika.' This is the horizontal exit, reaching the other shore directly from here, like the fragrant elephant cutting across the stream—attained in a single thought. Hence this function and power is the most excellent.

blocks.text: Next, the reason for the brief annotation, in two parts. First, the proper account, in three parts. First, the reason for the broad explanation.

inline.s: [Commentary] The scripture is concise and the Buddha's intent is profound and subtle; though recitation and upholding are many, careful study is truly rare.

[Sub-commentary] This sutra does not exceed a thousand words, yet it fully expresses the purport of a Pure Land that is the mind and an Amitābha that is the self-nature. One may truly say the scripture is concise and the Buddha's intent profound and subtle. Moreover, the World-honored Amitābha is especially related to the Sahā beings, so that those who hear this teaching all accept it with joy and reverence. Add to this that the sutra's words are simple and its practice easy, and it meets the capacity of beings for easy faith; hence both clergy and laity recite, read, and uphold it. Yet the text being clear is easy to glimpse, while the principle being deep is rarely investigated; this causes the Buddha's intent to be obscured and not revealed. Then the explanations of the former worthies could not but be broad.

blocks.text: Next, the reason for the brief explanation.

inline.s: [Commentary] Only the writings of the former worthies are lamented as rarely heard by the later ages.

[Sub-commentary] The writings of the former worthies are listed separately after the preface. Masters such as Ci'en and Gushan each had their compositions—some with expansive words, some with profound and subtle principles, all unbefitting the first-stage practitioner; hence they are rarely heard in later ages. Therefore the present brevity cannot but be put forth.

blocks.text: Third, the proper account of the brief explanation, in two parts. First, the account of the modest spirit.

inline.s: [Commentary] Presumptuously imitating the circulation of the teaching, I briefly set forth my citations.

[Sub-commentary] 'Circulation': the Golden Light commentary says, 'Flowing is the name of pouring down; circulating is the name of not being blocked.' The wish is that the water of the right Dharma should, from this present time, pour down to the future, and that the trap and the net of the holy teachings should not be blocked in ages to come. The Great Master speaks humbly: privately I have imitated the ancients in circulating the great Dharma, and therefore briefly set forth my citations, drawing on the established words of the various explanations to form the brief explanation. Yet in the process I sometimes use the meaning without the wording, abbreviate the expression but not the intent, in order to complete a single school's utterance, as if it came from one person's pen—one may call this a felicitous mode of authorship.

blocks.text: Next, the account of his own vow.

inline.s: [Commentary] I wish, with like-minded companions, universally to bind the pure affinity and all to realize non-birth, together ascending to non-retrogression. Such is my humble claim.

[Sub-commentary] The first two lines present a private understanding for the benefit of others—binding with like-minded companions the pure affinity of the Buddha's land broadly. The next two lines apply one's own aspiration to all beings—according to those who hear, to realize and ascend to the station of non-birth and non-retrogression. This is precisely the bodhisattva's resolve to benefit self and others, the mind of the awakened one's great compassion in its vast succor.

blocks.text: Fourth, the appended account.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Tang Master Ci'en composed a Comprehensive Praise of Amitābha in one scroll; the Song masters Gushan, Jingjue, and Lingzhi each had commentaries and notes; the masters Lun of Sanqu and Xin of Gu'ai each wrote collected annotations. Now wishing to follow the brief for the ease of first-stage practitioners, I set them aside separately, each following his own intent.

[Sub-commentary] 'The Tang Master Ci'en' onwards sets forth the ancients' annotations; 'now wishing to follow the brief' onwards sets forth his own annotation. Since this sutra is so widely recited, the annotations and commentaries must be many. Those now cited, that fall within my reading and hearing, are only the six masters by count. Those I have recently seen further include the sectioned commentary of Master Zong Yuexi, the sectioned explanation of Master Puzhi in the Hongwu period of the present dynasty, and the commentary-annotation of the recent Master Lianchi. If the brief is to be followed, this explanation is the most so. As for wishing wide reading, that too is to be followed by each according to his own intent.

inline.s: [Commentary] To explain this sutra-title by the five-fold profound meaning: following Master Gushan, take the fruit-person of the two lands as the name, the Vaipulya real-form as the substance, faith, vows, and pure karma as the cardinal purport, the forsaking of suffering and the obtaining of joy as the function, and the Great Vehicle of raw ghee as the doctrinal classification.

[Sub-commentary] 'The five-fold' are name, substance, cardinal purport, function-power, and doctrinal classification. 'Profound' means abstruse and hard to see; 'meaning' means deeply so with a reason. This is the Tiantai Great Master Zhiyi, who deeply entered the Buddha's mind and thoroughly illumined the scripture's intent: before explaining the scripture-text, he first takes that which is abstruse and hard to see, that which is deeply so with a reason, and uses it to explain the scripture-title, so that one who casts a glance at the title at once knows the scripture's meaning. For the name is the scripture's name; the substance is what the scripture-name expresses—the mind-substance of living beings; the cardinal purport is the practice—raising the contemplation-directive from the whole nature-substance and returning the whole contemplation-practice to the cardinal purport of the mind-substance; the function-power is the great function of the scripture's substance and purport in generating goodness and destroying evil; the doctrinal classification clarifies the advancement and the suitability of the Tathagata's teaching in the five periods. The intent is to make students, by the name, seek the mind-substance; by the substance, establish the cardinal purport; by severing doubt, generate faith; by generating goodness, destroy evil; and to know well the great and the small, the one-sided and the round, so that they do not mistakenly confound the scripture's intent.
