inline.s: [Commentary] 'The Buddha speaks': Śākyamuni, the teaching-lord, proclaims with the four unobstructed eloquence.

[Sub-commentary] 'Buddha' is the generic title of the supreme sage. To raise his particular title, he is the teaching-lord of the Sahā world, fully called Śākyamuni, which here means 'the Able One, the Silent One.' The Able One is his function; the Silent One is his substance. Here the wisdom lies in speaking, which is his teaching-function; hence the substance is set aside and the function followed, and he is titled 'the Able One,' able in his compassion to benefit the three realms. The four unobstructed are: first, unobstructed eloquence in meaning—knowing the meaning-principle of all dharmas, penetrating without obstruction; second, unobstructed eloquence in dharmas—penetrating the names of all dharmas, discriminating without obstruction; third, unobstructed eloquence in expression—for the names and meaning-principles of dharmas, fitting all beings in their different regions and languages, he speaks so that each and all may understand, discriminating without obstruction; fourth, unobstructed eloquence in delight in speaking—fitting the root-natures of all beings and the dharmas they delight to hear, speaking them in perfect accord without obstruction. Whenever the Buddha teaches, he proclaims with these four unobstructed eloquences; hence it is called 'the Buddha speaks.'

blocks.text: Second, the separate explanation of the two characters, in two. First, the explanation of the character 'Buddha.'

inline.s: [Commentary] The Sanskrit 'Buddha' is in Chinese 'the Awakened One,' one of the ten titles. One who has ultimately awakened and realized the real-form of all dharmas is called 'the Perfect Awakening.'

[Sub-commentary] The title calls him 'Buddha'; the Sanskrit is abbreviated, the full form being 'Buddha,' which in Chinese is 'the Awakened One,' belonging to person. If one says only 'Buddha,' the Chinese translation is 'awakening,' belonging to dharma. The generic titles are ten: first, Tathagata; second, Worthy of Offerings; third, Rightly and Universally Knowing; fourth, Perfect in Illuminated Conduct; fifth, Well-departed; sixth, World-knower; seventh, Supreme Person; eighth, Taming Husband; ninth, Teacher of Gods and Humans; tenth, Buddha. Having the ten titles complete, he is honored in the world. 'One who has ultimately awakened and realized' and so on points to the Tiantai six identities; in judging the Buddha, it is the sixth, the ultimate identity, the awakening. The six identities are: first, the awakening of the principle-identity; second, the awakening of the name-identity; third, the awakening of the contemplation-conduct-identity; fourth, the awakening of the semblance-identity; fifth, the awakening of the partial-truth-identity; sixth, the awakening of the ultimate-identity. Because there are six, ordinary beings and sages are not confounded, avoiding the rise of the great pride [of falsely deeming oneself supreme]; because there is identity, beginning and end are not two, avoiding the rise of discouragement. The first, the awakening of the principle-identity: the real-form of all dharmas is perfectly endowed in a single mind; the blind and the dull do not diminish it, and inversion and delusion do not damage it. Hence the verse of Wujizi: 'In movement and stillness the principle is complete; in conduct and in repose all matters are wrong. Darkly one follows things away, and vaguely does not know the return.' This is called the awakening of the principle-identity. The second, the awakening of the name-identity: from a good spiritual friend or from the sutras one hears the names of the three jewels and knows the words of the four truths to be wholly thus, without a hair's difference. Hence Wujizi's verse: 'Just now I heard the song of non-birth; only then did I hear the gatha of deathlessness. Now I know the whole is thus, and regret my former idling.' This is called the awakening of the name-identity. The third, the awakening of the contemplation-conduct-identity: with the whole principle of the three truths one raises the contemplation-practice of the three contemplations, universally subduing the five abodes and entering the station of the five grades. Hence the verse: 'Thought after thought illumines the constant principle; mind after mind stills the dust of falsehood. Universally contemplating the nature of dharmas, there is neither the provisional nor the true.' This is called the awakening of the contemplation-conduct-identity. The fourth, the awakening of the semblance-identity: though not yet formed as a vessel, the coarse defilements first fall away; one sees the semblance-principle and obtains purity of the six faculties. Hence the verse: 'Though the four abodes are first shed, the six dusts are not yet all empty. There is still a film in the eye, and red flowers are seen within the void.' This is called the awakening of the semblance-identity. The fifth, the awakening of the partial-truth-identity: partially breaking ignorance and partially seeing the Buddha-nature, becoming Buddha in the hundred realms and completing the way in the eight appearances. Hence the verse: 'Suddenly the mind opens in understanding; brightly and serenely all is penetrated. Yet the source is not exhausted; one still sees the moon indistinctly.' This is called the awakening of the partial-truth-identity. The sixth, the awakening of the ultimate-identity: ignorance is completely broken and the virtue of the three qualities is fulfilled; tracing the source to the very bottom, one is called the Supreme Person. Hence the verse: 'From of old the true was false; today all falsehood becomes true. One merely revives the original nature, and there is not a single dharma that is new.' This is called the awakening of the ultimate-identity.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the character 'Shuo,' in two. First, the glossing explanation.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Shuo' also means to delight. Meeting the capacity and speaking, it is called the delighting of the Buddha's heart.

[Sub-commentary] Siming says: 'Delight is the flowing delight; the breast is the mind's embrace. To speak of this sutra: it is the Tathagata's long-cultivated and long-realized Buddha-recitation samādhi, stored within his breast. Now that the capacity has knocked and aroused it, in speaking there is the flowing forth of what was formerly held within.'

blocks.text: Second, the distinguishing explanation.

inline.s: [Commentary] Moreover, a sutra may commonly be spoken by five kinds of persons; distinguishing it from the bodhisattvas, gods, sages, and transformed beings, therefore it is said 'the Buddha speaks.'

[Sub-commentary] The five persons can all speak sutras; if they request the Buddha's seal, they may all be handed down. Distinguishing it from the other four, it is therefore marked 'the Buddha speaks.'

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of 'Amitābha,' in two. First, the translation of the Sanskrit.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Amitābha' here means 'Immeasurable Life.'
[Sub-commentary] The three characters 'Amitābha' are Sanskrit; in this land they are translated 'Immeasurable Life.'

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two. First, the explanation of 'Immeasurable Life,' in two. First, citing the scripture to explain.

inline.s: [Commentary] The scripture says: 'That Buddha's life-span, and that of his people, are immeasurable and unbounded asamkhyeya kalpas.'

[Sub-commentary] 'That Buddha's life-span' raises the teaching-lord; 'and his people' raises the living beings. In that Pure Land, though there are its people, there is no king. Because its people each take the good as their own rule and need no joint civil and military governance, there is no king; there is only the Buddha as the teaching-lord, the Dharma-king. In general, the life-span of a teaching-lord follows the life-span of the land's people to fix its length. In that land the people's life is still immeasurable; how much more the Buddha's life—could it be measured? This raises the people to reveal the lord: the Buddha's life is immeasurable.

blocks.text: Third, the comparative-superior explanation.

inline.s: [Commentary] Since the response-body is immeasurable, and even the gods and humans do not know its number, how much more the Dharma-body and the Reward-body!

[Sub-commentary] The Dharma, Reward, and Response bodies each have their life-span and measure. Now life is established depending on the life-principle, and the life-principle is sustained by the body. Since the scripture speaks of life and also of body and life-principle, the Tiantai Great Master, in his commentary on the Contemplation Sutra explaining the title 'Immeasurable Life,' illumines the three bodies, three life-principles, and three life-spans, saying: 'The Dharma-body takes the dharma-nature as its teacher-and-rule, and also takes the dharma-nature as its body. This body is neither material form nor mind-intellect, nor is it held within the aggregates, realms, and senses; it forcibly points to the dharma-nature as the Dharma-body. The life of the dharma-nature is not the life-root obtained by retribution, nor does it have a continuous holding; it forcibly points to the unchanging and unmoving as 'life.' This life is neither long life nor short life, neither extended nor shortened; it forcibly points to the dharma-realm as equal to the expanse of empty space. This is the body that is no body, the life that has no life, the measure that is no measure. The Reward body is what cultivation brings about; the Lotus Sutra says it is obtained by long cultivation of karma, and the Nirvāṇa Sutra says the Great Parinirvāṇa is obtained by the practice of the way. The thusness-wisdom illumines the thusness-realm; bodhi-wisdom responds to and merges with the dharma-nature. To respond is like a lid matching its box; to merge is like water and milk merging. The Dharma-body is no body and not-no-body; the wisdom like-wise merging is no body and not-no-body; it forcibly names this wisdom the Reward body. The dharma-life is no life and not-no-life; the wisdom likewise responding and merging is no life and not-no-life; it forcibly names the not-life as life. The dharma-measure is no measure and not-no-measure; the wisdom likewise responding and merging is no measure and not-no-measure; it forcibly names the no-measure as measure. The Response body is the body that responds identically to all things: that which responds identically to the continuous as life; that which responds identically to the long and short as life. When the wisdom is merged with the substance, it can rise to great function, like quicksilver blended with true gold, which can smear over the various forms; merit is blended with the Dharma-body, and everywhere it responds by appearing and going forth. It can be a body and no-body; it can be a constant life and an impermanent life; it can be measureless and can be measured. To be measured has two senses: first, the measure that is measureless; second, the measure that is measured. Such as the seven hundred asamkhyeyas and the eighty years is the measured measure. Such as Amitābha, who truly has a limit yet is beyond the counting of gods and humans, is the measured that is measureless. Responsive Buddhas all have these two measures, following things and conditions, in varying lengths. Yet these three bodies and three lifes cannot be placed side by side as distinct; one-ness or difference would violate the dharma-substance. They are one yet three, three yet one—this accords with the profound text. Now the present text uses the response-life to indicate by comparison the Dharma and the Reward; and on that account the sutra-title is called 'Immeasurable Life.'

blocks.text: Next, the explanation of 'Immeasurable Light,' in two. First, the separate translation.

inline.s: [Commentary] It is also called 'Immeasurable Light.'

blocks.text: Second, citing the scripture.

inline.s: [Commentary] The scripture says: 'That Buddha's light is immeasurable, illumining the lands of the ten directions with no obstruction.'

[Sub-commentary] This too is the light of the response-body of the Immeasurable Life Buddha. Using the light to illustrate the life, the response can likewise be discussed in its three bodies: the Dharma-body is no body and not-no-body, so the Dharma-light is no light and not-no-light, and so on. Now this is the light of the response-body, and yet it is immeasurable, illumining the lands of the ten directions without obstruction—how much more the Dharma and Reward lights!

blocks.text: Second, the explanation in terms of the generic and the particular titles, in two. First, the proper explanation.

inline.s: [Commentary] Moreover, 'Buddha' is the generic title, and 'Amitābha' is the particular title.
[Sub-commentary] All Buddhas have both a generic and a particular title. In the title of this sutra, Śākyamuni raises only the generic, and Amitābha raises only the particular.

blocks.text: Second, resolving the doubt.

inline.s: [Commentary] Śākyamuni is this land's teaching-lord, known to all beings everywhere, so the generic title is raised. Amitābha is the guiding teacher of the Land of Bliss; as a matter of principle he must be manifested, so the particular title is displayed.

[Sub-commentary] Someone may doubt: since the Buddhas have both generic and particular titles, why did the sutra-title not raise the two lands' teaching-lords, generic and particular together, so as to say, 'The Buddha Śākyamuni speaks the Amitābha Buddha Sutra'? Therefore the explanation resolves the doubt: 'Śākyamuni is this land's teaching-lord, whom all living beings have heard and known; so only the generic title is raised, to include its particular. Amitābha is the guiding teacher of the Land of Bliss; if his particular were not manifested, his name would not be shown; so the particular title is displayed, to include its generic.' The translator, to spare repetition and preserve the brief, has fittingly placed it.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the generic title, in two. First, the explanation in terms of dharma and constancy.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Sutra' means dharma and constancy: the ten realms alike follow it, and the three times do not change it.

[Sub-commentary] This explanation of dharma and constancy is drawn from the commentary on the Contemplation Sutra by a transferred explanation, and again from the Miaozong Chao: the Confucian classics, in their exposition, have these two glosses—'the rule of conduct for ten thousand generations,' hence glossed as dharma; 'not changed by a hundred kings,' hence glossed as constancy. The Buddhist sutras are the same: the ten realms all take them as the rule, and the three times do not change them.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation by the reason of the meaning.

inline.s: [Commentary] Because it is proclaimed from the golden mouth of the sage, it is therefore called a sutra.
[Sub-commentary] The Miaozong Chao says: 'Because the Buddha, the great sage, from his golden mouth proclaims the dharma that he himself has realized, it is therefore called a sutra.'

blocks.text: Second, the combined explanation of the generic and the particular, in two. First, pointing to the two names, generic and particular.

inline.s: [Commentary] Moreover, 'sutra' is the generic name, and 'the Buddha speaks' and the rest are particular names.

[Sub-commentary] Miaozong says: 'As to the generic name: whether sudden or gradual sayings, provisorily set up or provisorily opened, apart from the vinaya and the treatises, all are called sutras; hence it is called generic. As to the particular names: the particular forms are many. Here they follow three—person, dharma, and simile: three single, three double, and one complete, forming the seven particular types. The three single are: single person, as in the Amitābha Sutra and so on; single dharma, as in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra and so on; single simile, as in the Brahma-net Sutra and so on. The three double are: person and dharma, as in the Manjusri Asks about Prajñā Sutra; dharma and simile, as in the Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma; person and simile, as in the Tathagata's Lion's Roar Sutra. The complete one of person, dharma, and simile is as in the Srimala Lion's Roar Single-Vehicle Great Skillful Means Vaipulya Sutra. With these seven particular names combined with the generic, the whole of the Buddha's teaching is marked out.'

blocks.text: Second, making clear the reason of the generic and the particular, in five. First, the general discussion of a single transformation.

inline.s: [Commentary] The sutra has three kinds: teaching, practice, and principle. Relying on the teaching one cultivates the practice, and from the practice one reveals the principle.

[Sub-commentary] Miaozong says: 'Our school, in explaining the title, discusses it in terms of the generic and the particular because these two names each contain teaching, practice, and principle. Without these three, merely discussing the generic and the particular has no basis. Why? Because relying on the teaching one thereafter cultivates the practice, and from the practice one thereafter reveals the principle.'

blocks.text: Second, pointing separately to the present title.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Buddha' means awakening; spoken in terms of what cultivation accomplishes, it belongs to practice. 'Speak' is teaching. 'Amitābha' is principle.

[Sub-commentary] In the present title the character 'Buddha' is judged to belong to practice, because 'Buddha' means awakening, which has the sense of self-awakening and awakening others, and awakening and practice both complete. Spoken from the side of cultivation's completion, it belongs to practice. The character 'speak' belongs to teaching, most clearly. 'Amitābha' is judged to belong to principle, because it is the Amitābha of the self-nature: it is precisely as the practitioner, invoking, reciting, and cultivating, that one sees him; therefore it is judged to belong to principle.

blocks.text: Third, judging the generic and the particular.

inline.s: [Commentary] Different from the many scriptures, then the three sutras are all particular. In relation to the character 'sutra,' then the three sutras are all generic.

[Sub-commentary] Different from the many scriptures, then not only do the five characters form the particular, but also the three scriptures of teaching, practice, and principle are all particular. In relation to the character 'sutra,' not only does the single character form the generic, but the three scriptures of teaching, practice, and principle are all generic.

blocks.text: Fourth, concluding as the secret treasury.

inline.s: [Commentary] Principle is the Dharma-body, practice is prajñā, teaching is liberation. The three in one perfectly fused and inconceivable are called the secret treasury.

[Sub-commentary] Whenever our school explains a sutra-title, it always does so in terms of the generic and the particular precisely to make clear that each separately contains the three scriptures. And that each separately contains the three scriptures is again precisely to make clear that it contains the secret treasury. As in a single title, the three characters 'Amitābha' are the Dharma-body—the self-nature of me the practitioner; the one character 'Buddha' is the prajñā-wisdom that rises to cultivation from the whole nature; the one character 'speak' is the liberation obtained through the wisdom and the Dharma-body. Again, principle is the whole path of suffering as the Dharma-body, the Buddha-nature of the primary cause; practice is the whole delusion as prajñā, the Buddha-nature of the illuminating cause; teaching is the whole karma as liberation, the Buddha-nature of the circumstantial cause. These three virtues are like the three dots of the character 'I' or the three eyes of the heavenly king: neither vertical nor horizontal, neither side by side nor separate. They are the inconceivable secret treasury. The meaning-principle of the sutra-title is so subtle. How could teachers and listeners overlook it?

blocks.text: Fifth, concluding as merit.

inline.s: [Commentary] Hence hearing the title-name at the head attains immeasurable merit.
[Sub-commentary] As in the Golden Light sutra and the various Great Vehicles, this is often said.

blocks.text: Second, bringing forth the original name.

inline.s: [Commentary] The original name of this sutra is 'Praise of the Inconceivable Merit, the Sutra Guarded and Recollected by All Buddhas.'

blocks.text: Third, distinguishing the differences in translation, in three. First, the general statement.

inline.s: [Commentary] Handed down to China, there are two translations in all.

blocks.text: Second, the separate statement, in two. First, the Tang translation.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Tang translation says 'The Sutra of the Buddha's Reception of the Praised Pure Land.'

blocks.text: Second, the Qin translation, in two. First, distinguishing its difference from the Tang.

inline.s: [Commentary] The present Qin text conceals and abbreviates the sutra-title; after the Buddhas of the six directions it immediately says, 'You living beings should believe this, and so on.'
[Sub-commentary] The Tang translation retains the original name, while the Qin translation does not, because it is concealed and abbreviated, being placed after the Buddhas of the six directions.

blocks.text: Second, praising the Qin translation's skill.

inline.s: [Commentary] Because this sutra properly shows the method of holding the name, and moreover the holy name of Amitābha is what all beings delight to hear, so by using it to establish the title many people believe and accept it. Hence it is universally observed in all the four seas and circulated without end. Such is the translator's skill.

[Sub-commentary] In general, establishing a name is valued for generating good in beings. Here the good generated is of two kinds: first, this sutra properly shows the method of holding the name; second, the holy name of Amitābha is what all beings delight to hear. Hence, by using it to establish the title, many people believe and accept it. Wherefore the Tang translation lies hidden in the great treasury, unseen and unheard, while the Qin translation is universally observed in the four seas and circulated without end. The translator's skill is trustworthy and has evidence.

blocks.text: Second, distinguishing the substance, in two. First, the statement of the heading.

inline.s: [Commentary] Second, distinguishing the substance.

[Sub-commentary] 'Second, distinguishing the substance' is that which in the earlier general list was said: 'The Vaipulya real-form is the substance.' The Vaipulya real-form has two senses. First, this sutra was spoken in the third, the Vaipulya period, when the four teachings of the Vaipulya are all discussed together, and this sutra belongs to the Round; it distinguishes that this sutra's real-form is not the real-form of the Avatamsaka, Prajñā, or Lotus periods—hence it is called Vaipulya. Again, the real-form of the Round teaching: every gate can enter the pool of coolness; hence 'fang' (the expanded). Living beings and Buddhas both possess it, equal and non-dual; hence 'deng' (the equal). The commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says, 'The substance is the essential substance.' The Miaozong Chao says, 'The name is on the side, a guest; the substance is the main, the host. The name is a provisional name; the substance is the real substance. Every name has beneath it its substance. Now we distinguish the real substance beneath the provisional name.'

blocks.text: Second, the explanation, in two. First, citing the treatise to make clear the substance.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Treatise of Great Wisdom says: 'All Mahayana sutras universally take the single real-form as their proper substance.'

[Sub-commentary] The Miaozong Chao says: 'All dharmas are unproduced and unextinguished, neither existent nor non-existent, neither a doer nor an object; they leave the characteristics of words, leave the characteristics of names, leave the characteristics of the mind's conditions. Leaving these characteristics is called the real-form, the form of the formless.' If we bring back that meaning to this sutra, then the first section from 'seven rows of railings' down to 'those who hear this sound all give rise to the thought of the Buddha, the thought of the Dharma, and the thought of the Sangha' makes clear the Pure Land that is the mind—what the preface calls 'the bejeweled groves and jade-like pools directly reveal the mind-source.' The middle section from 'For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha' down to 'It can only be spoken of as immeasurable, unbounded asamkhyeyas' makes clear the Amitābha of the self-nature—what the preface calls 'the measure of longevity and the light fully manifest the self-nature.' 'The bejeweled groves and jade-like pools' reveals the dependent retribution, which includes the four kinds of Pure Land; 'the measure of longevity and the light' and so on reveals the proper retribution, which includes the Buddhas and bodhisattvas and the people of the nine grades of rebirth. This is precisely the Lotus teaching's 'only the Buddha and the Buddhas can exhaust the real-form of all dharmas'; it is what Tiantai calls 'the nature endowed with the three thousand, none of which is outside the substance of the real-form.'

blocks.text: Second, concluding what is expressed.

inline.s: [Commentary] This is the principle expressed.

blocks.text: Third, making clear the cardinal purport, in two. First, the statement of the heading.

inline.s: [Commentary] Third, making clear the cardinal purport.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation, in two. First, citing the scripture to establish it.

inline.s: [Commentary] The scripture says: 'If there be one who believes, he should make the vow to be reborn in that land.'

[Sub-commentary] In the earlier general list it was said that faith, vows, and pure karma are the cardinal purport. Hence now the scripture is cited to establish it. 'If there be one who believes' is the gate of faith. 'He should make the vow' is the gate of vows. To establish the practice-gate of pure karma, one should also cite the following passage, 'Holding the name for seven days, single-minded and unconfused, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.' These are the gates of the three essentials. Faith is the faith that there is a Pure Land that is the mind, an Amitābha that is the self-nature, and the Tathagata's vow-power, through which all may attain rebirth. This corresponds to the first of the ten vehicles, 'contemplating the inconceivable realm.' Though there be this faith, if there is no vow, one cannot be reborn. For since Amitābha by his vow-power already gathers living beings, I should make the vow to seek rebirth, so that there is the natural relation of the essential nature and the effortless giving and taking away, like a magnet naturally attracting. Judged among the ten vehicles, this is the second, 'truly giving rise to the bodhi-mind.' Among the four universal vows, when it is 'the Buddha way is supreme, and I vow to accomplish it,' this includes the three preceding vows. Though there be this vow, if there is no practice-gate, the vow becomes wild. Hence one must hold the name for seven days, single-minded and unconfused. Gathering this within the ten vehicles, it is the third, 'skillfully settling the mind in calming and insight.' Holding the name for seven days is insight; single-minded and unconfused is calming. Just at the moment of holding the name is the single mind; just at the moment of the single mind is the holding of the name. Thus calming and insight both illumine and both suspend; in skillfully settling the mind, one achieves it. This briefly marks out the three methods for those of superior faculties; the remaining seven vehicles are all included within them.

blocks.text: Second, concluding as the cardinal purport.

inline.s: [Commentary] This is the cardinal purport of the whole sutra.

blocks.text: Fourth, making clear the function, in two. First, the reminder.

inline.s: [Commentary] Fourth, discussing the function.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation, in two. First, citing the scripture to establish it.

inline.s: [Commentary] The scripture says: 'They immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Bliss, and all are non-retrogressing from supreme bodhi.'

[Sub-commentary] The first two lines show the passage after 'Holding the name for seven days, single-minded and unconfused.' The next two lines are the earlier scripture's 'Those reborn there are all avivartika.' The earlier general list said that the forsaking of suffering and the obtaining of joy is the function, which is the scripture's text 'they immediately attain rebirth' and so on. If we use the later to complete the earlier, then 'those reborn there' are all the Sahā beings who practice Buddha-recitation, and they must attain non-retrogressing bodhi. These two passages together establish the function and power of this sutra.

blocks.text: Second, concluding as the function and power.

inline.s: [Commentary] To depart from the suffering of birth-and-death and obtain the joy of liberation: this is the function and power of this sutra.

[Sub-commentary] The other gateways all cause living beings to exit the three realms vertically, departing the suffering of birth-and-death and obtaining the joy of liberation—like a nine-story tower from which one ascends higher and higher; when the strength is sufficient one advances, and when the feet tire one falls, so the ascent is difficult. Only the Pure Land gateway causes living beings to exit the three realms horizontally, departing the suffering of birth-and-death and obtaining the joy of liberation—like a home's threshold, from east to west; a glance and it is seen, a snap of the fingers and one is there, so the going is easy. Is not the function and power of this sutra great?

blocks.text: Fifth, judging the doctrinal classification, in two. First, the general statement.
Fifth, judging the doctrinal classification.

inline.s: [Sub-commentary] 'Teaching' is the sage's words addressed to those below; 'classification' is the distinguishing of same and different. The Tathagata established the teaching in the five periods, advancing according to the time; the great and the small, the gradual and the sudden, each have their divisions. Tiantai distinguishes them according to the five periods, and each has its rationale. Hence whenever one explains a sutra, one must judge its doctrinal classification.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the classification.

inline.s: [Commentary] The division belongs to the Mahayana Vaipulya teaching; according to the meaning of the two storehouses, it is included in the bodhisattva-storehouse; dividing gradual and sudden, it belongs to the sudden teaching.

[Sub-commentary] In judging this doctrinal classification there are three statements. 'The division belongs to the Mahayana Vaipulya teaching' is the first, judging by the period. The earlier general list said that the Mahayana raw ghee is the doctrinal classification; raw ghee is the Vaipulya period. The Tiantai Great Master used the Nirvāṇa five periods, in their arising order, to judge the whole teaching of the Tathagata's single transformation. First, from the cow comes milk—an analogy for the Buddha's very first, in the twenty-one days, preaching the Avatamsaka Sutra. Next, from milk comes curds—an analogy for the twelve divisions bringing forth the nine divisions of sutras, and for the twelve years in which he preached the four Agamas of the lesser vehicle. Next, from curds comes raw ghee—an analogy for the Agamas bringing forth the Vaipulya; in eight years he preached the Vimalakirti, the Great Collection, the Surangama, the Lankavatara, the sixteen Contemplations, and this sutra, refuting the one-sided and censuring the lesser, extolling the greater and extolling the Round. The shravakas obtain the benefit of the refutation and rebuke, ashamed of the lesser and aspiring to the greater, entering and departing without difficulty. For example, the lesser vehicle's one-sided emptiness, outside the three realms, has no body and no land; now he specially tells Shariputra that Amitābha has a land, the bodhisattvas have a body, and those reborn there are all non-retrogressing—this is precisely that matter. Next, from raw ghee comes ripened ghee—an analogy for the Vaipulya bringing forth the Prajñā; in twenty-two years he preached the great Prajñā and other sutras, using the water of the emptiness-wisdom to wash away the two-vehicle practitioners' attachments, causing Subhuti and others to turn and teach the Prajñā, bestowing the wealth and melting it together. Next, from ripened ghee comes the finest cream—an analogy for the Prajñā bringing forth the Lotus and the Nirvāṇa; the nine realms and the three vehicles are united in the provisional and given the prophecy, with none small and none great, all caused to become Buddhas. Now this is the third, raw ghee; hence it is said that the division belongs to the Mahayana Vaipulya teaching. 'According to the meaning of the two storehouses, it is included in the bodhisattva-storehouse' is the second, judging by the storehouse. The sutras spoken by the Buddha include the shravaka-storehouse—those spoken for the two-vehicle practitioners—whose principle reaches only the true truth, whose delusion only breaks views and thoughts, whose wisdom only cultivates the emptiness-contemplation, and whose fruit has no body and no land. Since this sutra makes clear that apart from the Sahā there is a separate Pure Land, then its fruit-reward has a body and a land; is it not that its principle, delusion, wisdom, and fruit all belong to the bodhisattva-storehouse? 'Dividing gradual and sudden, it belongs to the sudden teaching' is the third, judging by the teaching. The teachings of the transformation-manner are gradual and sudden. The gradual requires eons of cultivation to reach non-retrogression; the sudden accomplishes it in this very life, reaching the station of avivartika. Hence it concludes: 'to cause ordinary beings not to retreat from bodhi.' Yet to cause them in this very life to reach the station of non-retrogression is indeed a Round and Sudden teaching; but one must first open the Round understanding, then cultivate the Round practice, break the three delusions, and then realize the Round fruit, in order to reach non-retrogression. Now it merely speaks of the proper and dependent retribution of that land, to serve as the opening of understanding and the generating of faith; and the holding of the name for seven days, single-minded and unconfused, to serve as the gateway of practice; and at the end of life, immediately attaining rebirth, to reach non-retrogression. Unless it were Śākyamuni's skillful means, Amitābha's vow-power, the practitioner's past roots, the three essentials at present, and single-mindedness unconfused in fully subduing and at once cutting off the three delusions and the root of karma, and advancing straight ahead without turning—how could one accomplish this? Hence know that this sutra is the supreme cream for the evil world of the five turbidities. The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: 'Poison placed in raw ghee; eating it at once kills.' How could one not believe it?

blocks.text: Second, the translator, in two. First, the statement of the section.
Second, the translator's title.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumarajiva of the Yao Qin, by imperial command
Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two. First, making clear his birthplace.

inline.s: [Commentary] Kumarajiva, here meaning 'Child-lifespan,' was a man of the kingdom of Kucha.

blocks.text: Second, making clear his translation.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Later Qin's Yao family held Chang'an, honored him as the national teacher, and in the Hongshi period he translated the various sutras and treatises.

[Sub-commentary] 'Yao Qin' distinguishes it from the fallen Qin, the Former Qin, and the Qifu Qin; this is the Later Qin of the Yao family. It was in the third year of Hongshi that he entered Chang'an. The Qin lord commanded the monk Xian and others, eight hundred shramanas, to receive Kumarajiva's instruction. At the Caotang Temple he translated sutras and treatises, in all ninety-eight works, comprising four hundred twenty-one scrolls; Sengrui, Sengzhao, Daochang, and others took down the translation.

blocks.text: Third, attesting to his merit.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Nanshan Gan Tong Zhuan says: 'The sutra-translating master since the seven Buddhas.'

[Sub-commentary] The past seven Buddhas all were born in western India, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu. After their nirvāṇa, whether in the period of the right Dharma or of the semblance Dharma, the Sanskrit texts of the West were sure to be transmitted to China, and translated from Sanskrit into Chinese. Translating masters have existed in every age; only Master Kumarajiva, from the time of the seven Buddhas, has always been the sutra-translating master for our China. This was said by the Nanshan Vinaya Master on the question put by Master Fei, the celestial being. Some also say that Master Kumarajiva's station attested to the three worthies. Hence we know he was no ordinary man.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the scripture-text, in two. First, the total and separate sectioning; second, the explanation according to the sections. Now the first has two. First, the total sectioning into three divisions.

Second, the scripture-text in three divisions. From the beginning to 'the great assembly were all gathered' is the preface division. From 'At that time the Buddha told' to after the six directions, where the scripture-title is adduced and explained, is the main-teaching division. From 'You should all believe and accept my words' to the end of the text is the circulation division.

inline.s: [Sub-commentary] Since the Han Ming Emperor, when the sutras came to China, those who spread the teaching expounded them following the text, without any sectioning. It was the Jin Master Dao'an who first divided the greater and lesser sutras, all having three divisions—the preface, the main teaching, and the circulation. Later, when the western sastra on the Bodhisattva's Illumination arrived, its three divisions accord with this. Again, the renunciates of this land since the Han all followed their teacher's surname, as with the three Zhi. Later Master Dao'an said that since one has left one's lay surname to follow Śākyamuni, all should be joined under the single surname 'Shi.' Later, when the Ekottara Agama arrived, the World-honored One indeed said: 'A thousand streams entering the sea all have one salty flavor; the four castes that leave home are all called Śākyamuni's descendants.' Hence later people praised Master Dao'an: 'His division of the sutras well accords with the sastra of light; his conferring the surname Shi is much like the Ekottara.'

blocks.text: Second, the separate statement of the two prefatory divisions.

inline.s: [Commentary] All sutras have both the common and the separate prefatory divisions. This sutra has only the common preface—the attestation of faith—and no separate preface of initiation; it is, among the twelve divisions, the 'taught without being asked.'

[Sub-commentary] The two prefatory divisions: 'common' means the same—the six matters such as 'Thus have I heard' are the same in all sutras; hence 'common.' 'Separate' means the different—the initiating circumstances of each sutra are different. Hence this sutra has only the common preface and no separate preface, being the Tathagata's spontaneous teaching without a question. For the Pure Land teaching, if it were aimed at the bodhisattva capacity, it would be precisely what they face and must be spoken upon a question—as in the sixteen Contemplation Sutra, which is such a case. But this sutra is addressed to the supreme vehicle and to the capacities of ordinary beings, to make them know that a subtle body and land are to be obtained in this very life. This was originally not the realm of the lesser vehicle or of ordinary beings; how could they ask of it? Hence the Tathagata, without being asked, spoke it spontaneously, proclaiming in accord with his nature—what need of an initiating circumstance?

blocks.text: Second, the explanation according to the sections, in two. First, the explanation of the common preface, in two. First, the division into sections.
The common preface is in two. First, the five sentences of attestation.

inline.s: [Sub-commentary] 'Attestation of faith': as the Buddha was about to pass into nirvāṇa, Ānanda asked, 'At the head of all sutras, what words should be placed?' The Buddha replied, 'Place the words “Thus have I heard” and so on.' Not only I do this—the Buddhas of the three times all open their sutras in this way.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the scripture, in two. First, setting forth the scripture.

inline.s: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anathapindada, in the kingdom of Shravasti.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in five. First, the explanation of the dharma-substance indicated.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Thus' points to the dharma-substance heard. The principle of the real-form, the same in ancient and modern times, is called the principle of thusness, and is spoken as 'is.'

[Sub-commentary] 'Thus' is a word pointing to the dharma. What it points to is the dharma-substance heard—the principle of the real-form. Such a principle, the same in ancient and modern times, is called 'thus,' that is, the unmoving substance of suchness, traversing the ten thousand ages yet ever new, passing through a thousand differences yet unchanging. The Tathagata can weigh this principle and speak, without ever being contrary to it; hence it is called 'thus.'

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the one who hears, that is manifested.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'I' is Ānanda, who at the compiling of the dharma-treasury said of himself, 'This dharma-gate, I heard from the Buddha.'

[Sub-commentary] The Buddhabhumi Sastra says: at the time of compiling, they jointly requested, saying, 'As you have heard it, so should you speak.' The dharma-transmitting bodhisattva then consented, saying, 'Thus shall I speak, as I have heard.'

blocks.text: Third, the explanation of the capacity and response that are made clear.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'At one time' is the time when the capacity and the response unite. The reason a specific year, month, or day is not stated is that the two lands' calendars differ.

[Sub-commentary] The capacity is Ānanda and the twelve hundred, together with the bodhisattvas and the rest; the response is Śākyamuni Tathagata, the able teaching-lord. Without the response the capacity cannot be accomplished, and without the capacity the response cannot be fulfilled; only when the anvil and the mallet strike together is the vessel formed. When the capacity and the response are united, then this sutra is spoken. 'The two lands' calendars differ'—as with the four seasons of this land versus the three times of the other, or East China reckoning the first of the month by the dark of the moon, while the West reckons it by the full moon. Since the two regions are thus, one can infer for the four border peoples; it is hard to fix, so it says only 'at one time.'

blocks.text: Fourth, the explanation of the teaching-lord named.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Buddha' means awakening. Self-awakening differs from the non-awakening of ordinary beings; awakening others differs from the solitary awakening of the two vehicles; the completion of awakening differs from the bodhisattvas in their causal stage. Honored among the many sages, he is therefore called the Buddha—that is, Śākyamuni the teaching-lord.

[Sub-commentary] The Sanskrit 'Buddha' here means 'the Awakened One'—one who has awakened to the nature and the characteristics, the true and the false—that is, the ultimate original awakening and the ultimate initial awakening. 'Self-awakening differs from the non-awakening of ordinary beings': ordinary beings are dazed and disturbed all day, following falsehood and drifting; the Tathagata is serene and illumined in merged union, reverting to the source and returning to the root. 'Awakening others differs from the solitary awakening of the two vehicles': the two vehicles, having awakened to birth-and-death, leap alone like a stag; the Tathagata himself reaches the other shore and, in his compassionate ferry, ferries beings across. 'The completion of awakening differs from the bodhisattvas in their causal stage': the bodhisattvas, though cultivating the three awakenings, have not completed the three causes; the Tathagata has completely fulfilled the three awakenings and perfectly manifested the three virtues. Being honored among the two-vehicle practitioners and the bodhisattvas, among the many sages, he is called the Buddha. Following the particular from the generic, he is the Sahā teaching-lord, Śākyamuni Buddha.

blocks.text: Fifth, the explanation of the abode described, in two. First, the explanation of the kingdom of Shravasti.

inline.s: [Commentary] Shravasti, properly Sravasti, here means 'the land of renown,' spoken of because its people and things were wealth-abundant and famous far among the kingdoms.
[Sub-commentary] 'Its people and things were wealth-abundant' means this kingdom was complete in the things of the sense-desires and wealth, and abundant in those who heard much and were liberated.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anathapindada, in two. First, setting forth the names and virtues of the two persons, in two. First, Jeta.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Sanskrit 'Jeta' here means 'victory'; it is the name of the prince of King Prasenajit.
[Sub-commentary] When the prince of King Prasenajit was born, it chanced that they had just won a victory over a foreign kingdom; hence this fine name was given.

blocks.text: Second, Sudatta.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Sanskrit 'Sudatta' here means 'good giving'; it is the name of an elder, who could bestow gifts on the poor of the land and was named 'the giver to the orphaned and solitary.'

blocks.text: Second, making clear the joint naming of the two persons.

inline.s: [Commentary] He spread gold sideways to buy the garden from Jeta, established a monastery, and invited the Buddha to teach; Jeta donated the trees; hence the two are named together.

[Sub-commentary] The elder Sudatta, arranging a marriage for his son, went to Rajagrha and there saw the Tathagata; he invited the Buddha to accept offerings. The Buddha told Shariputra to go with him to look at a site. Only Prince Jeta's park, with its flourishing trees, could be made into a monastery. Jeta jestingly consented: if he covered the ground with gold bricks laid sideways, and hung the forest with gold coins, then he would give it. Sudatta, delighted, had carts carry gold to spread over the ground, nearly filling it. Jeta, seeing his sincerity, said, 'The ground should belong to you; the trees belong to me. Let us together offer them to the Buddha—would that not be good?' Hence afterwards, whenever a sutra was spoken at this place, the compilers of the sutra, setting forth the location, always praise the virtue of the two and name them together.

blocks.text: The listing of the assembly that heard together, in two. First, the division into sections.
Second, the listing of the assembly that heard together, in three. First, the shravaka assembly, in two. First, showing the number.
Second, the explanation of the scripture, in three. First, the shravakas. Second, showing the number, in two. First, setting forth the scripture.

inline.s: Together with the great assembly of bhiksus, twelve hundred and fifty persons, all great arhats, well known to the multitude.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in four. First, the explanation that makes clear the class.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Bhiksu' here means 'alms-mendicant': he begs food to sustain the body and begs the Dharma to refine the mind. It also means 'one who frightens Mara' and 'one who destroys evil.' 'Sangha,' fully 'samgha,' here means 'the harmonious assembly.'

[Sub-commentary] 'Bhiksu' is Sanskrit and contains three meanings. First, an alms-mendicant: outwardly he begs food from benefactors to sustain the material body, forever leaving the four wrong ways of livelihood; inwardly he begs the Dharma from the Tathagata to refine the mind-nature, ever tending toward the eight-fold right path; this is the cause of being worthy of offerings. Second, one who destroys evil: he can destroy the ninety-eight kinds of the evil causes of affliction and the evil fruits of birth-and-death of the twenty-five existences; this is the cause of the slayer of thieves. Third, one who frightens Mara: when he gives rise to the resolve to leave home, Mara is frightened at his leaving the realm; when he diligently cultivates, [the evil one] is frightened at the cause of leaving desire and non-birth. 'The harmonious assembly': whoever is a monk must have the six harmonies—first, harmony of precepts, cultivating together; second, harmony of views, understanding together; third, harmony of body, dwelling together; fourth, harmony of benefits, sharing equally; fifth, harmony of speech, without disputes; sixth, harmony of mind, delighting together. Possessing these six harmonies, one may be called a sangha.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation showing the number.

inline.s: [Commentary] The three Kashyapas had a thousand disciples, and Sariputra and Maudgalyayana together two hundred and fifty; these first took refuge in the Buddha and are the ever-attendant assembly.

[Sub-commentary] The three Kashyapas are: first, Uruvilva Kashyapa; second, Gaya Kashyapa; third, Nadi Kashyapa. If one adds the first five, Kaundinya and the others, the sum is twelve hundred and fifty-five persons; the sutra gives the round number and so abbreviates it. None before them tasted the nectar of the teaching; hence they are the ever-attendant assembly.

blocks.text: Third, the explanation revealing the station.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Arhat' contains three meanings. First, worthy of offerings: the field of merit for gods and humans, the fruit of the alms-mendicant. Second, slayer of thieves: having destroyed affliction completely, the fruit of the destroyer of evil. Third, non-birth: not receiving future existence, the fruit of the frightener of Mara.

[Sub-commentary] 'Bhiksu' is the causal name; 'arhat' is the fruition title. The two names, cause and fruit, each correspond one-to-one, like a shadow following the form, without the slightest error. Thus being a bhiksu, one has the cause of the alms-mendicant, and only then obtains the fruit of the arhat, worthy of offerings, the field of merit. One has the cause of destroying evil, and only then obtains the fruit of having destroyed affliction completely, the slayer of thieves. One has the cause of frightening Mara, and only then obtains the fruit of non-birth, not receiving future existence.

blocks.text: Fourth, the explanation praising the virtues.

inline.s: [Commentary] Hearing the name and revering the virtue is called 'knowing'; seeing the form and respectfully serving is called 'recognizing.'

[Sub-commentary] If one has only heard the name but not seen the form, then one 'knows' but does not 'recognize.' If one has only seen the form but not heard the name, then one 'recognizes' but does not 'know.' Now since they have heard the name and seen the form, they must revere the virtue and respectfully serve. The Venerable Ānanda heard together with these persons; this does not merely show that the virtues of those in the same rank are equal, but also reveals that the Dharma he heard is true. Using this to attest the faith, it is indeed trustworthy.

blocks.text: Second, the listing of the names, in two. First, the reminder of the section.
Second, the listing of the names.
Second, the explanation of the scripture, in two. First, setting forth the scripture.

inline.s: The elders Shariputra, Maha Maudgalyayana, Maha Kashyapa, Maha Katyayana, Maha Kaushthila, Revata, Suddhapanthaka, Nanda, Ānanda, Rahula, Gavampati, Pindola Bharadvaja, Kalodayin, Maha Kapphina, Vakkula, and Aniruddha.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two. First, the explanation of 'elder.'

inline.s: [Commentary] Advanced years and great virtue are commonly called 'elder.'

[Sub-commentary] Among these holy monks, one who has advanced years must have great virtue, but one who has great virtue is not necessarily advanced in years. Hence 'elder' is the common title for advanced years and great virtue.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the sixteen names. First, the explanation of Shariputra.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Shariputra' here means 'son of the body.' His mother's bodily form and features were upright, her eyes like those of the heron; combining her name, he is also called 'the son of the heron.' Foremost in wisdom.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of Maudgalyayana.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Maha Maudgalyayana' here means 'the great of the bean-gatherers,' a surname. His clan being numerous, he is distinguished by 'great.' Foremost in supernormal powers.

blocks.text: Third, the explanation of Maha Kashyapa.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Maha Kashyapa' here means 'of the great turtle clan'; his ancestor was moved to see a spiritual turtle bearing forth a sage's chart, and so named the clan. It is also called 'drinker of light,' because his body's light was blazing and outshone the light of others. In the time of Vipashyin Buddha he was a metalworker; a poor girl, with a gold bead, helped him together build a stupa and an image; from that time his body's light has been golden.

blocks.text: Fourth, the explanation of Maha Katyayana.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Maha Katyayana' here means 'graceful ornament.' Foremost in discussion.

blocks.text: Fifth, the explanation of Maha Kaushthila.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Maha Kaushthila' here means 'great knee,' named from his appearance. He was Shariputra's maternal uncle.

blocks.text: Sixth, the explanation of Revata.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Revata' here means 'constellation.' His parents prayed to the stars and he was born; hence it was taken as his name.

blocks.text: Seventh, the explanation of Suddhapanthaka.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Suddhapanthaka' here means 'continuing the path.' His mother, going to visit her relatives, gave birth at the roadside; hence his natural disposition was dull and slow. Yet by reciting only half a verse he realized the arhat fruit.

blocks.text: Eighth, the explanation of Nanda.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Nanda' here means 'good joy'; he was the Buddha's own younger brother.

blocks.text: Ninth, the explanation of Ānanda.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Ānanda' here means 'rejoicing.' Son of King Shuddhodana and the Buddha's younger cousin, he was born on the day the Buddha attained the Way; the whole realm rejoiced, and for that reason this fine name was established. Foremost in hearing much.

blocks.text: Tenth, the explanation of Rahula.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Rahula' here means 'the obstructor'; it was originally the name of an asura that could obstruct the sun and moon. The Buddha being obstructed, he did not immediately leave home; hence this was taken as his name.

blocks.text: Eleventh, the explanation of Gavampati.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Gavampati' here means 'the cow's rumination.' In a former life he was a cow, and after eating he would ruminate; hence he received this name.

blocks.text: Twelfth, the explanation of Pindola Bharadvaja.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Pindola' here means 'unmoving,' a name; 'Bharadvaja' here means 'sharp faculties,' a surname. Another translation says 'Pindola Bharadvaja.'

blocks.text: Thirteenth, the explanation of Kalodayin.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Kalodayin' here means 'black light,' because his form was coarse and black.

blocks.text: Fourteenth, the explanation of Kapphina.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Maha Kapphina' here means 'the constellation of the chamber'; his mother prayed to the chamber star and he was born.

blocks.text: Fifteenth, the explanation of Vakkula.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Vakkula' here means 'good appearance'; his form and features were upright. Formerly he gave a single myrobalan to the monks, and obtained the retribution of not dying five times.

blocks.text: Sixteenth, the explanation of Aniruddha.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Aniruddha' here means 'not poor.' Formerly, in a time of famine, he gave coarse food to a pratyekabuddha; for ninety-one kalpas his fruition was abundant. Foremost in the divine eye.

[Sub-commentary] All sutras, in listing the assembly, praise the virtues—as in the Lotus and the Surangama, which are instances. Only this sutra does not; yet it is not that there is none. It is because the translator, in his skill, caused them to reflect on the name and consider its meaning. Such as the great-wisdom Shariputra and Maha Maudgalyayana—what virtues are not manifest? Yet when the sutras praise virtue, it must follow the occasion. For example, Ānanda, by the condition of the defiling affair, stirred the Surangama assembly, and the compiler of the sutra, in praising virtue, said especially: 'The son of the Buddha, dwelling and upholding, well arise in all existences.' Those in the same rank having this virtue shows precisely the one aimed at: though he relied on the condition of defilement, in truth he had no such fault. The remaining disciples of this sutra need not be discussed; even the great-wisdom Shariputra, placed at the head, and next the great Maudgalyayana, Maha Kashyapa, and Maha Katyayana—could these four have been without intention? For the Land of Bliss teaching: without the bodhisattva's actual wisdom none can believe; without the bodhisattva's great supernormal powers none can reach it; without shaking off the three delusions none can be pure; without the four unobstructed eloquence none can discuss it. This sutra was spoken in the Vaipulya period, its intent being to cause the shravakas to turn the lesser wisdom into great wisdom, the lesser supernormal powers into great ones, the lesser ascetic practice into great asceticism, the lesser discussion into great discussion. 'The Pure Land, being provisional yet actual, actual yet provisional'—with this one can illumine and understand the real-form, believe it, receive it, and practice it. 'Being near yet far, far yet near'—with this one can, without haste, be swift, and arrive at a snap of the fingers. 'The mind pure and the land pure, defiled yet pure'—with this one can have birth yet non-birth, birth and transformation both merging. 'Wonderful being is emptiness, true emptiness is being'—with this one can exercise the wonderful eloquence and analyze without obstruction. As for the remaining disciples, each has one virtue; by kind praising the virtue and by the matter dedicating it, toward this teaching they accomplish the Vaipulya benefit: understanding non-birth while being born, sensing the birth outside the realms; reaching the body that is no body while receiving the transformation body. The vertical exit from the three realms is indeed inconceivable; and there is the horizontal exit from the three realms, which is even more inconceivable.

inline.s: Such as these many great disciples.

inline.s: [Commentary] Learning follows after the teacher, hence called 'disciple'; understanding is born of the teacher, hence called 'son.' This concludes the foregoing text.
[Sub-commentary] 'Younger brother' shows the teacher's humility; 'teacher' sets forth the disciple's reverence. Hence the Master said: 'I treat Hui as a younger brother; Hui treats me as a father.'

inline.s: And all the bodhisattvas, the great beings.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Sanskrit 'bodhisattva' here means 'an enlightened being.' Being the same realization as the Buddha is called 'awakened'; not having exhausted ignorance is called 'sentient being.' 'Mahasattva' here means 'a being of the great bodhi-mind.'

[Sub-commentary] The two characters 'bodhisattva' are an abbreviated Sanskrit. If fully stated, it should be 'maha-bodhi-citta-sattva.' 'Maha' is translated 'great,' 'bodhi' 'way,' 'citta' 'mind,' 'sattva' 'being' (also translated 'sentient'); combined, 'a being of the great bodhi-mind.' With the great bodhi-mind it differs from beings below; with 'sentient' it differs from the Buddhas above. For they have already left this shore yet are still in the midstream. These bodhisattvas are those who further dwell in the great among them; hence they are distinguished by 'mahasattva.'

inline.s: Manjusri, prince of the Dharma; the bodhisattva Ajita; the bodhisattva Gandhahasti; the bodhisattva of Constant Advance; and such great bodhisattvas as these.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in five. First, the explanation of Manjusri.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Manjusri' here means 'wonderful virtue,' because the subtle three virtues are the same as what the Buddha realized. He is also called 'the bodhisattva of wonderful auspiciousness.' Having entered the right station of the Dharma, he is called 'prince of the Dharma.'

[Sub-commentary] 'The subtle three virtues, the same as what the Buddha realized': in the Round teaching, from the first abode to the stage of equal enlightenment, one breaks a portion of ignorance and partially shares the Buddha's realization of the subtle three virtues. As for Manjusri bodhisattva, there is the distinction of his fundamental and his manifested. His fundamental cause—as in the Karuna-pundarika sutra—was that, before the Jewel-Treasury Buddha, he made the vast, grand vow, received the Buddha's prophecy, and was named Manjusri. Again, in the time of Dipankara Buddha he was the teacher of the eight princes and was the ninth-generation ancestor of Śākyamuni. Formerly he was near to the Buddhas; now he assists Śākyamuni. As for his fundamental fruit: at present, in the northern region he is a Buddha in the World of Joy, named the Buddha of the Treasury of Jewels, the Store of Joyfulness; in the future, in the southern region, in the World Free of Defilement, he will become a Buddha, named the Tathagata Universally Manifest. His fundamental and manifested are thus; sharing the Buddha's realization, his station is equal. He is also called 'wonderful auspiciousness': the three of delusion, karma, and suffering have a remnant, none yet auspicious. His station being ultimate, the three virtues are fully manifested; hence he is also titled 'wonderful auspiciousness.' The Buddha broke through the twenty-five existences, attained the king-samādhi, and entered the proper station of the Dharma, being called the Dharma-king who destroys existence. Manjusri likewise, in a station adjacent to equal enlightenment, is the eldest son of the Buddha, called 'prince of the Dharma.'

blocks.text: Next, the explanation of Ajita.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Ajita' here means 'unconquered,' transcending the one-sided and the lesser; hence it is the name of the Maitreya clan.

[Sub-commentary] The Sanskrit 'Ajita' is translated 'no one can overcome,' a name. He is also called 'Maitreya,' translated the compassionate clan, a surname. The Surya-samādhi sutra says: 'If living beings see him, they at once attain the compassion-mind samādhi.' Combined, this bodhisattva has, by his station, realized and entered the stage adjacent to the ultimate, and his compassion-mind reaches beings; hence he received this name and surname.

blocks.text: Third, the explanation of Gandhahasti.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Gandhahasti' here means 'not resting,' because he diligently cultivates without slackening.

[Sub-commentary] The Suramgama-samādhi sutra says: 'Taking a Ganges-sand number of kalpas as a day and night, thirty such as a month, and twelve months as a year; passing a hundred, thousand, myriad, ko?i of kalpas, one meets a Buddha. Thus meeting a Ganges-sand number of Buddhas, practicing the pure conducts and cultivating merit, then receiving the prophecy—his mind does not rest.' Hence he is called Gandhahasti.

blocks.text: Fourth, the explanation of Constant Advance.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Constant Advance' is so because the dharma-nature is ever-present, accomplishing the effortless right diligence.

[Sub-commentary] The Ratnakuta sutra says: 'This bodhisattva, for the sake of all living beings, through immeasurable kalpas, follows after them without abandoning; and even if they do not accept the transformation, he does not have a single thought of forsaking. With both body and mind advancing, he is called Constant Advance.' It is only because he sees the dharma-nature as ever-present that he accomplishes the effortless right diligence; though he advances, there is no characteristic of advancing.

blocks.text: Fifth, the explanation of the general conclusion.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Great bodhisattva' because they far transcend the one-sided and the lesser.

[Sub-commentary] Lingzhi says: 'The name bodhisattva is common to the beginning and the end. These bodhisattvas are all of the deep station of the one-birth to Buddhahood, or else provisionally manifested as influence; hence they are called great.' The sutras, in listing the bodhisattva assembly, also praise the virtues, as in the Lotus and so on, which is their general practice. Only this sutra does not; yet it is not that there is none. It is also to cause those who read this sutra to reflect on the name and consider its meaning, to revere the virtue and receive the practice. Why? As Manjusri, with wonderful virtue and auspiciousness; Ajita, with no one able to overcome; Maitreya; Gandhahasti, with self-strengthening without rest and diligent cultivation without slackening; Constant Advance, with the realization that the dharma is ever-present and the accomplishing of the effortless right diligence—what virtue is not possessed? The compiler of the sutra lists only these four, the intent being to cause those who cultivate the Pure Land, first, to take the subtle three virtues—the three truths of my mind—as the basis of the three contemplations, i.e., what is called 'first contemplate the inconceivable realm.' Next, to follow with the unconquered unconditioned compassion and truly give rise to the bodhi-mind, to signify that those who now seek rebirth in the Land of Bliss take as their first resolve to transform living beings, sever afflictions, study the dharma-gates, and accomplish the Buddha way. Then, adding to it the whole-nature-arising-cultivation, self-strengthening without rest, diligent cultivation without slackening, and realizing the ever-present dharma-nature so as to accomplish the effortless right diligence—then one can exhaust the forsaking of the impure and penetrate to the source of the pure; from the obstruction of the Sahā one can reach the penetration of the Land of Bliss. Then the practice-grades will naturally be harmonized, the antidotes will of themselves assist the opening, the nine grades may be attained, the City of Doubt not dwelt in, the love of Dharma not arising, and the golden platform may be ascended. One may join the ranks of such great bodhisattvas as these. Is not this the compiler's intent?

inline.s: And Shakra, lord of the gods, with immeasurable hosts of gods and the great assembly, were all gathered together.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in three. First, the explanation of Shakra.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Shakra-devānām-indra' here means 'the able heavenly lord'; he is the lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven.

[Sub-commentary] The Sanskrit, fully stated, is 'Shakra-devānām-indra,' translated 'the able-doer heavenly lord,' the lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven. 'Trayastrimsa' is translated 'thirty-three.' On the summit of Mount Sumeru, on the four sides there are in all eight cities, each city dwelling four gods; the lord of gods dwells in the Sudarshana city; together they are thirty-three. The adornments of cause and fruit are fully set forth in the verses of the Treasury of Abhidharma.

blocks.text: Next, the explanation of the immeasurable gods.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The immeasurable gods' are the Brahma lords and the four world-protecting kings in the desire and form realms, and so on.

[Sub-commentary] The desire realm has six heavens: the two earth-dwelling, namely the four king-heavens below together with the second, the Trayastrimsa heaven; and the four space-dwelling, namely Yama, Tushita, Nimmanarati, and Paranirmitavasavartin. The form realm has four heavens: the first dhyana, the second dhyana, and the third dhyana each have three heavens, and the fourth dhyana has nine heavens. Whenever the Buddha teaches, they all come and gather. Only the formless-realm heavens, having no material substance, are not said to come.

blocks.text: Third, the explanation of the great assembly.

inline.s: [Commentary] Including the four assemblies and the eight classes, hence it says 'the great assembly were all together.'

[Sub-commentary] 'The four assemblies' are monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. 'The eight classes' are gods, nagas, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and humans and non-humans.
