inline.s: At that time the Buddha told the elder Shariputra: 'Passing from here to the west through a hundred thousand ko?i of Buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhavati, the Land of Bliss.'

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in six. First, the explanation of 'at that time.'

inline.s: [Commentary] 'At that time' is the time when the sutra was about to be spoken.
[Sub-commentary] 'At that time' is the earlier common preface's time when the capacity and the response were united. Only because they were united was the sutra about to be spoken.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the one aimed at.

inline.s: [Commentary] Because Shariputra had sharp faculties, he told him specifically, without waiting for his question.

[Sub-commentary] Jingjue says: 'Not telling the bodhisattvas, the gods, and the nagas—there should be four intents. First, he is the disciple on the left side, who in both the great and small assemblies of the Dharma often stands at the head. Second, because he is foremost in wisdom, and the four assemblies and eight classes all revere him. Third, to cause the four assemblies, hearing of the Buddha's Pure Land, to feel shame at their own lack of a share. Fourth, again to cause the lesser vehicle, who have not yet attained realization, to turn their minds to the great.' Whenever the Buddha teaches, he must obtain the benefit of the four siddhanta. Now I say that among the twelve divisions of the Buddha's teaching, this is the 'taught without being asked,' because the Pure Land teaching is not the realm of the lesser vehicle; and again it desires to cause them to turn from the lesser to the great. This sutra only omits the geya, the gatha, the nidana, the avadana, and the upadesha; while the long prose, direct discourse, vaipulya, the vyakarana, and the adbhuta-dharma are all shown to be present. As for the jataka and the itivritaka—to look from the brief to the vast, in the larger Amitābha sutra these too are present.

blocks.text: Third, the explanation of the number of lands.

inline.s: [Commentary] One great-thousand world is called one Buddha-land. The Treatise of Ten Doubts says: 'The West is a hundred thousand ko?i of lands away from here merely as spoken to the ordinary being's fleshly eye and to the measure of the birth-and-death mind. But if living beings accomplish the pure karma, then the mind in samādhi at the end of life is the mind that is reborn in the Pure Land; the arising of thought is the time of birth in the Pure Land—it is truly not far.'

[Sub-commentary] In the explanation, first the distance is made clear according to the scripture; next the not-far is made clear according to principle. 'One great-thousand world is called one Buddha-land': a hundred ko?i of suns and moons, a hundred ko?i of Sumerus, a hundred ko?i of great oceans, a hundred ko?i of iron rings—this is called one Buddha-land. Hence the Abhidharma verse says: 'The four great continents, sun and moon, Sumeru, the six desire heavens, and the Brahma world, each to the number of a thousand, are called one small-thousand world. A thousand times this small-thousand is called the middle-thousand world. A thousand times this is the great-thousand—all with one arising and one destruction.' Viewed thus, the Land of Bliss is very far from here. Next the Tiantai Great Master's Treatise of Ten Doubts makes clear the not-far. For ordinary beings, because of the retribution of prior-life afflictions, delusion, and good and evil karma, obtain this life's aggregate-fruit of suffering; all their fleshly eyes cannot see far, and they take the unseen as far; and all their birth-and-death mind cannot know far, and they take the unknown as far—no wonder it is so. But if a person who invokes the Buddha is single-minded and unconfused, then the delusion is subdued; if the pure karma is accomplished, then the karma-path is pure. At the end of life, when the seal of the Sahā is broken, then the suffering-path is released. At that moment the fleshly eye is transformed into the divine eye, and the ordinary mind is changed into the sage-mind. Hence the mind in samādhi at death is the mind reborn in the Pure Land; the arising of thought is the time of birth in the Pure Land. 'The arising of thought' means that at the point of death one sees the three jewels, or sees the light, or sees the lotus, and so on; once there is some seeing, it is called the arising of thought—not a thought of false thought. Though still in this land, to have seen is already the time of being reborn in the lotus-pool; hence it is said 'truly not far.' Again, the Pratyutpanna sutra makes clear that living beings have three powers by which they see Amitābha. First, the samādhi-power, which is what the treatise explains. Second, the Buddha-power: the forty-eight vows—the scripture says, 'If I become Buddha, and living beings of the ten directions, with sincere mind and joyful faith, wish to be born in my land, even to ten recitations—if they are not born, may I not attain the right awakening.' Third, the fundamental merit-power. This has two senses: first, living beings from beginningless time have had the seed of invoking the Buddha and seeking birth in the Pure Land; at that time it did not arise, but now the seed has ripened, so they should attain rebirth. Second, the mind-nature of living beings originally contains the dust-lands; though the distance be a hundred thousand ko?i, it is all the endowment of the nature. That is, the nature-substance and the nature-measure are like a single jewel in the net of Indra, reflecting the many jewels; or a single wave of the great sea, containing the whole tide-substance. Not only do they mutually contain, they are mutually identical. Hence Siming says: 'If the mind-nature did not contain the dust-lands, then beings would have no function of sensing and seeing, and the Buddha would have no principle of responding and appearing.'

blocks.text: Fourth, the explanation of 'Utmost Bliss.'

inline.s: [Commentary] The Sanskrit 'Sukhavati' here means 'the Peaceful Nourishing'; or 'Clear and Tranquil'; and again 'Utmost Bliss'—that is to say, 'the most excellent.'

[Sub-commentary] 'Peaceful Nourishing' is in contrast to the Sahā, where the eight sufferings are mutually stewed, so what is nourished is not peaceful. 'Clear and Tranquil' is in contrast to the Sahā's evil world of the five turbidities, so where one dwells is not tranquil. 'Utmost Bliss' is in contrast to the Sahā's extremity of many sufferings, so what is received is not blissful.

blocks.text: Fifth, setting forth the four lands, in two. First, the general statement.

inline.s: [Commentary] All lands, as sensed according to capacities, are of four kinds.

blocks.text: Second, the separate explanation of the four. First, the Still-Light land.

inline.s: [Commentary] First, the land of Everlasting Still-Light, where the ultimate final fruit of the Buddhas dwells.

[Sub-commentary] The commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: 'Everlasting Still-Light: the everlasting is the Dharma-body, the still is liberation, the light is prajñā. These are the three dots of 'I,' neither vertical nor horizontal, called the secret treasury.' The Miaozong Chao says: 'The first three are in matter, so the land's name is set by the dweller's cultivation, severance, cause, and fruit. This land belongs to principle, so it is named from the three virtues of the substance itself.' I privately say: since in the commentary there is already the name of the higher grade of Still-Light, one knows that that land too is divided into nine grades; only the highest grade is where the ultimate fruit dwells, and the remaining eight grades are where the Round sages with partial realization dwell—this is the partial-realization Still-Light. The commentary says 'partial and ultimate, the purity and impurity of Still-Light'—this is it.

blocks.text: Second, the Real Reward land.

inline.s: [Commentary] Second, the Real Reward land, where the great beings of the Dharma-body dwell.

[Sub-commentary] The commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: 'The Real Reward and Non-obstruction: practicing the true dharma, one senses the superior reward; form and mind do not obstruct each other, hence 'non-obstruction.' It is purely bodhisattvas, with no two vehicles.' The Benevolent King sutra says, 'The three worthies and the ten sages dwell in the fruition-reward'—this is its meaning. The Great Wisdom Treatise says, 'The superior, wonderful five desires of the bodhisattva can cause Kashyapa to dance.' The Avatamsaka says, 'Immeasurable fragrant-clouds platforms'—that is the pure, wonderful five objects of that land. I privately say: the Buddhas also have a reward-land; why must it be that only the bodhisattvas dwell there? One may also, by analogy, divide it into nine grades: the highest grade where the Buddha dwells, and the remaining eight grades following the more or less ignorance the bodhisattvas have broken, as the differentiation. The commentary says 'successive and sudden entry, the purity and impurity of the Real Reward'—this is it.

blocks.text: Third, the Expedient land.

inline.s: [Commentary] Third, the Expedient land, where the three-vehicle persons dwell.

[Sub-commentary] The commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: 'The Expedient Remainder: cultivating the expedient way, one severs the four abode delusions, hence 'expedient'; ignorance not yet exhausted, hence 'remainder.'' The Great Wisdom Treatise says, 'Outside the three realms there is a Pure Land where shravakas and pratyekabuddhas are born, receiving the dharma-nature body, not the divided birth.' The Lotus says, 'If after my parinirvāṇa one truly attains arhatship, but does not believe this Dharma, then meeting another Buddha, he will be settled.' Among these there are further the sharp and the dull, the upper being pure and the lower impure. I privately say: since it says 'within it there are further the sharp and the dull, the pure and the impure,' then by analogy it too is divided into nine grades: the Round expedient way dwells in the upper three grades, the Separate and Shared expedient way in the middle three grades, and the Tripitaka expedient way in the lower three grades. The commentary says 'substance and analysis, the skillful and the clumsy; the purity and impurity of the Remainder'—this is it.

blocks.text: Fourth, the cohabitation land, in two. First, bringing forth the name.

inline.s: [Commentary] Fourth, the cohabitation land, where the six ordinary realms dwell.

[Sub-commentary] The commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: 'The Sahā is mixed and evil, thorns and tiles, full of impurity—this is the impure cohabitation. The pools flow with the eight virtues, the trees are arrayed with the seven jewels, level next to nirvāṇa, all in the right-determination group—this is the upper-grade pure land where ordinary and sage dwell together.'

blocks.text: Next, the explanation of the meaning.

inline.s: [Commentary] By the weight and lightness of the five turbidities the pure and the impure are divided. The Sahā's five turbidities are heavy, so it includes the four evil destinies and the wheel of rebirth never rests. The Peaceful Nourishing's five turbidities are light, so it has only gods and humans, all attaining non-retrogression; hence it is called the Land of Utmost Bliss.

[Sub-commentary] 'By the five turbidities' marks out the Sahā; the explanation below is spoken at one stroke. The Sahā beings, because the causes of the five turbidities are heavy, are called the impure cohabitation; hence the retribution includes the four evil destinies. This is because within the affliction-turbidity the five dull defilements, following whichever is the stronger, drag them to be born in the four destinies. Since gods and humans are due to precepts and goodness, their afflictions are somewhat light. The Peaceful Nourishing's five turbidities are light because, being in the Sahā, they concentratedly cultivated the pure karma, lightening the five turbidities; hence they attain rebirth in the Land of Bliss and receive the retribution of gods and humans. Moreover, having reached that land, the dusty objects are light and pure and do not give rise to afflictions; so though they are gods and humans, all attain non-retrogression; hence it is called the Land of Utmost Bliss. Spoken further, the Land of Bliss is also divided into pure and impure: as in the Contemplation Sutra's nine grades and the Larger Sutra's three grades. Since the grades are divided high and low, what is seen is naturally different. Hence the Miaozong Chao says: 'As to the five turbidities being light and the cohabitation pure—this purity is very general. One must know the particular intent. Those of precepts and goodness, in the ordinary stations of the four teachings, can all cause the five turbidities to be light and sense the pure cohabitation; while the Round contemplation of the light turbidities senses a pure cohabitation whose proper and dependent are most pure, as the scripture says. From the contemplation of the ground onwards, each characteristic, compared with other sutras, cultivating the many good practices that sense the Peaceful Nourishing land, is most distinct.'

blocks.text: Sixth, distinguishing.

inline.s: [Commentary] Speaking to the full principle, only the ultimate Still-Light is the true Utmost Bliss.

[Sub-commentary] 'Speaking to the full principle' and so on: this distinguishes successively through the four lands. Thus the partial-realization Still-Light is still like the impure land's region of suffering. Only the land where the ultimate fruit-person dwells can be called the true Utmost Bliss. Hence the earlier preface first made clear 'the true source is non-dual,' saying 'the Still-Light is truly pure, originally with no distinction of suffering and joy'—this is what it means.

blocks.text: Second, the separate explanation, in two. First, the Dharma-body.

inline.s: [Commentary] First, the body of the dharma-nature, dwelling in the Still-Light land; body and land are one, called the secret treasury.

[Sub-commentary] The commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: 'The Dharma-body takes the dharma-nature as its teacher-and-rule and also takes the dharma-nature as its body. This body is neither material form nor mind-intellect, nor held within the aggregates, realms, and senses; it forcibly points to the dharma-nature as the Dharma-body.' The Miaozong Chao says: 'To take the dharma-nature as teacher and rule, and to explain the term dharma, one abandons the generic and follows the particular. Generically, both living beings and Buddhas take the dharma-nature as their rule; yet the nine realms, though they rule, violate it, like a person following a teacher without obeying his instruction. Only the Buddhas, from the first giving rise of mind, have followed the dharma-nature in cultivation, and now can ultimately merge with the dharma-nature. Hence the Great Sutra says, “That which the Buddhas take as teacher is called the dharma.” Because the dharma is constant, the Buddhas are also constant. Following the dharma-nature, they name the dharma their teacher; yet it is not truly a teacher distinct from the self-substance. So they take the very dharma that is the teacher as their body. Though it is called a body, it has already gone beyond the five aggregates, so it is neither material form nor mind-intellect. Form is the first aggregate, and mind-intellect the four aggregates; since it is none of the aggregates, it is also none of the realms and senses, and so none of the three categories that hold and govern. This already separates it from the divided and the transformation body, which show birth-and-death and are held by aggregates and so on. One may also take material form to distinguish the response, mind-intellect to distinguish the reward, and the three categories to distinguish the cause. Since it is none of these, how can it be described? For the sake of beings, it forcibly points to the dharma-nature as the Dharma-body. This is the body that can dwell. The land it dwells in is as explained above.'

blocks.text: Second, the Reward body.

inline.s: [Commentary] Second, the Reward body, dwelling in the Real Reward land.

[Sub-commentary] The commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: 'The Reward body is what cultivation brings about; the Lotus Sutra says it is obtained by long cultivation of karma; the Nirvāṇa Sutra says the Great Parinirvāṇa is obtained by the practice of the way. The thusness-wisdom illumines the thusness-realm; bodhi-wisdom responds to and merges with the dharma-nature. To respond is like a lid matching its box; to merge is like water and milk merging. The Dharma-body is no body and not-no-body; the wisdom likewise merging is no body and not-no-body; it forcibly names this wisdom the Reward body.' The Miaozong Chao says: 'Reward means requital. Cultivation is the cause, sensing the wonderful reward, which requites the cause. The Lotus attests the wisdom-virtue: the scripture says, “The light of wisdom illumines immeasurably, obtained by long cultivation of karma.” The Great Parinirvāṇa attests the severance-virtue. These two fruition-virtues requite the cultivating cause, hence they are called reward. When the reward is sensed, what is its appearance like? Hence a single dharma and two similes reveal it. Just as, the name being not different and the contemplated being differentiated, it is not called the thus-realm; if there is a realm outside the wisdom, it is not called thus-wisdom. Each having two thus's: the realm is thus as the wisdom, and the wisdom is thus as the realm. This realm and wisdom are therefore able to respond and merge. “Wisdom” is a generic name, so it is distinguished by the fruition-awakening, bodhi: it is the wisdom of the supreme bodhi, responding to and merging with the dharma-nature realm. First the box-and-lid simile illustrates the responding; fearing that one might think the box and lid, though matching at the edges, still have two forms, another simile, water and milk, illustrates the merging, so one knows that the initial and the fundamental are both the same awakening nature, whose substance is merged—exactly like water and milk. This reveals that outside the realm there is no wisdom, and outside the wisdom there is no realm, as is visible in water and milk. “No body” means not the response-Buddha's body with division and limits; “not-no-body” means not the reward-Buddha's body without division and limits. Again, “no body” is non-being, and “not-no-body” is non-emptiness; the Madhyamaka Dharma-body is the substance of the fundamental awakening. The initial awakening merges with this, and the merging too is forgotten; for the sake of accomplishment, it is forcibly named the reward-wisdom. The land is as before.'

blocks.text: Third, the Response-transformation body.

inline.s: [Commentary] Third, the Response-transformation body, dwelling in the non-dual land; following the capacities of the nine grades, what is seen differs.

[Sub-commentary] The commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: 'The Response body is the body responding identically to all things. Wisdom merged with the substance can rise to great function, like quicksilver blended with true gold, which can smear over the various forms; merit blended with the Dharma-body, everywhere responding and appearing. It can be a body and no body.' Yet these three bodies cannot be set side by side as distinct; one-ness or difference would violate the dharma-substance. They are one yet three, three yet one—this accords with the profound text. The Miaozong Chao says: 'Like a valley answering the echo, the great and the small follow the sound; like a mirror revealing the form, the pure and the ugly lie in the substance. Responding to the sensing of all things, it manifests the superior and the inferior body. The wisdom is the reward body, and the substance is the Dharma-body; these two merged, the application is without limitation. The superior color of true gold needs quicksilver blended with it before it can smear objects; wanting this one condition, the gold has no smearing use. The reward-wisdom merit, meeting with the Dharma-body, wherever there is a capacity there is nowhere it does not respond. What was above said of the reward concerns only the merging with the dharma, which is the self-enjoyment. Now what is shown is the descending response: taking the other-enjoyment constant response, set against the birth-body's impermanent response, to reveal the two traces of function. Hence body and so on are both set forth: “body” is the birth-body, which has division and limits, hence called a body; “no-body” is the reward, which has no division and limits, hence called no-body. The lesser Prajñā says, “The Buddha speaks of the no-body, which is called the great body.” The great body is the other-enjoyment body. The “other body” is that which, at a time, following capacity, is transformed and comes into being; it is identical in meaning to the response body, but its substance and function differ slightly. The response body, from the merged substance of the Dharma and reward, rises to the responding application; the transformation body, from the substance of the response body, rises to the transforming application—that is, from function making function. Further, from transformation producing transformation, the transformations are without end. The response body goes through the eight appearances from beginning to end; the transformation body arises and vanishes swiftly. “Dwelling in the non-dual land”: the reward body is the wisdom that attests, and the Dharma-body is the principle attested. Thus the Still-Light and the Real Reward are both the substance that can respond; the other-enjoyment land and the Expedient and cohabitation lands are all where the response body dwells. The capacities' conditions differ, having the nine grades, so they are seen as different; the Buddha's response is without difference, so the Still-Light and the Real Reward cut across into the three grades. Hence “non-dual.” One should follow the commentary on the Contemplation Sutra to judge the nine grades of the reborn persons; those who wish should go there and examine it. Again, the four lands each are divided into nine grades; sensing and seeing according to the land, the three bodies differ; following capacity, the four lands are different.'

inline.s: Shariputra, for what reason is that land called the Land of Utmost Bliss? The living beings of that country have none of the many sufferings, but receive the many joys; therefore it is called the Land of Utmost Bliss.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'That land' below raises the question; 'that country' below gives the general explanation. 'Have none of the many sufferings' means none of the sufferings of the three evil paths, the eight difficulties, and so on. Spoken in contrast to the Sahā's extreme suffering, it is called the Utmost Bliss.

[Sub-commentary] The Sahā world includes the six destinies. Gods, humans, and asuras are called the three good destinies, having precepts and goodness as their cause; hell, hungry ghosts, and animals are called the three evil destinies, having evil and transgression as their cause. 'Destiny' has the meaning of being able to lead: all beings, doing good karma, can be led to the places of gods and humans; doing evil karma, can be led to the places of hell and so on. Again they are called the three paths, named from the fruit: by evil karma one is led to the path of fire, the path of knives, and the path of blood. First, the hell destiny: this place is below the earth and within the iron-ring mountain, having the eight cold and eight hot hells and so on; beings who did extremely heavy evil karma fall into this destiny, hence called the hell destiny. Second, the hungry-ghost destiny has three kinds: those of exceedingly heavy karmic offense, who for eons do not hear the name of water or gruel; the next sort seek only the voided filth of the human world, pus, blood, and excrement; and the lowest sort, occasionally once filled, are driven by knives and staves to fill rivers and seas. Beings who did evil karma, because of avarice, are born in this destiny. Third, the animal destiny: wearing fur and horns, scales, shells, and feathers; four feet and many feet, with feet and without; on water, on land, and in the air. Beings who did evil karma, because of delusion, are born in this destiny. The eight difficulties are eight places that all obstruct. Though these eight places differ in the suffering and joy of their retribution, all cannot see a Buddha or hear the right Dharma, so they are collectively called the difficulties. First, the hell difficulty: as explained before; in hell, in the long dark night, one suffers without interruption, obstructed from seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, hence called a difficulty. Second, the animal difficulty: as before; in the animal destiny one suffers without end, obstructed from seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, hence called a difficulty. Third, the hungry-ghost difficulty: as before; in the hungry-ghost destiny one suffers immeasurably, obstructed from seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, hence called a difficulty. Fourth, the long-lived heaven difficulty: this heaven has five hundred kalpas as its life; it is the No-Thought heaven in the fourth dhyana of the form realm. 'No-thought' means its mind-consciousness does not act, like a fish in ice or a dormant insect. Non-Buddhist practitioners are often born there, obstructed from seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, hence called a difficulty. Fifth, the northern Uttarakuru difficulty: Uttarakuru in Chinese means the superior place, because this place's retribution is superior to the three continents of east, west, and south. Its people live a thousand years, not dying young; because they are attached to pleasure they do not accept transformation, so sages do not appear among them; they cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma, hence called a difficulty. Sixth, the blind, deaf, and mute difficulty: though such persons may be born in the central land, their karmic hindrances are deep and heavy; blind, deaf, and mute, their faculties are incomplete. They may meet a Buddha's appearance in the world, but cannot see the Buddha; though the great Dharma be spoken, they cannot hear it; hence called a difficulty. Seventh, the difficulty of worldly wisdom and clever eloquence: worldly people of perverse wisdom and sharpness only devote themselves to addictively studying the non-Buddhist scriptures, not believing in the world-transcending right Dharma; hence called a difficulty. Eighth, the difficulty of being born before or after a Buddha: when a Buddha appears in the world, he is the great guide, causing all beings to depart the suffering of birth-and-death and obtain the joy of nirvāṇa. Those with a karmic affinity meet him. Those born before or after a Buddha, because of heavy karma and thin conditions, neither see the Buddha nor hear the Dharma; hence the difficulty of being born before or after a Buddha. Now the many sufferings are the eight sufferings of the human world. First, the suffering of birth has five kinds. One, entering the womb: at the time the consciousness entrusts to the mother's womb, it is in the belly, cramped and impure. Two, the seed: the consciousness entrusts to the parents' remains; its seed follows the mother's breath going in and out, without freedom. Three, the growth: in the mother's belly, through ten months, scorched by inner heat, the form gradually completes, dwelling below the channel of life and above the channel of the ripe, sandwiched as in a prison. Four, the exit from the womb: at the first birth, cold and hot winds blow on the body, and clothes and the like touch the body; the skin is tender, as if pierced. Five, the kind: among humans there is wealth and poverty, high and low, and form has mutilation and beauty; this is called the suffering of birth. Second, the suffering of old age has two kinds. One, growth: from youth to prime, from prime to decline; strength wanes and movement is unquiet. Two, decay: the bloom leaving, decline coming; spirit decreases, life shortens daily, gradually approaching ruin; this is called the suffering of old age. Third, the suffering of sickness has two kinds. One, bodily sickness: the four elements are unbalanced, and the many diseases attack. If the earth-element is unbalanced, the whole body is heavy; if the water-element, the whole body is swollen; if the fire-element, the whole body is hot; if the wind-element, the whole body is rigid. Two, mental sickness: the mind holds suffering, sorrow, and grief; this is called the suffering of sickness. Fourth, the suffering of death has two kinds. One, death by sickness: through disease the life-span ends and one dies. Two, external conditions: meeting evil conditions, or encountering the perils of water and fire, and dying; this is called the suffering of death. Fifth, the suffering of separation from the beloved: those one constantly loves and cherishes are estranged and scattered, unable to dwell together; this is the suffering of separation from the beloved. Sixth, the suffering of meeting the hateful: those one constantly resents and hates, whom one originally seeks to keep far away, instead assemble; this is the suffering of meeting the hateful. Seventh, the suffering of seeking without obtaining: worldly things one's mind loves, sought but not obtained; this is the suffering of seeking without obtaining. Eighth, the suffering of the blazing five aggregates: the five aggregates are form, feeling, thought, activities, and consciousness. 'Aggregate' has the meaning of covering, being able to cover the true nature and prevent its revealing. 'Blazing' has the meaning of great: the many sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death gather together; hence the suffering of the blazing five aggregates. 'Spoken in contrast to the Sahā's extreme suffering, hence called the Utmost Bliss': the beings of the Land of Bliss have none of the above Sahā's various extremely-suffering matters, hence called the Utmost Bliss. If set in direct contrast: the beings of the Land of Bliss, in all the dusty objects their six faculties encounter, are all subtle and wonderful; form, sound, smell, taste, and touch all give rise to contemplative understanding and faith in the three jewels; hence there is no cause of the three poisons, and no works of evil transgression, and so no fruit of suffering of the three evil paths, and no obstruction of the three evil destinies. Hearing the Dharma and entering samādhi, they do not fall into no-thought, so there is no long-lived-heaven difficulty. Though receiving the utmost bliss, they are constantly transformed by the teaching, so there is no Uttarakuru difficulty. The six faculties are pure, sharp, and wise, so there is no blind, deaf, and mute difficulty. Those reborn there are all in the right-determination group, so there is no worldly-wisdom cleverness difficulty. Amitābha Buddha is now preaching the Dharma through immeasurable kalpas, and Avalokitesvara immediately fills his place, named the Buddha of Universal Light, Merit, King of Mountains—so there is no difficulty of being born before or after a Buddha. Entrusting the body within the lotus calyx, there is no suffering of birth. Cold and heat do not shift, so no suffering of old age. The body is not of the divided kind, so no suffering of sickness. The life-span is immeasurable, so no suffering of death. There is no father, mother, wife, or child, so no suffering of separation from the beloved. The hosts of superior good people assemble, so no suffering of meeting the hateful. Heavenly flowers and fragrant food are enjoyed of themselves, so no suffering of seeking without obtaining. Contemplating the aggregates as empty, there is no suffering of the aggregates.

inline.s: Moreover, Shariputra, in the Land of Utmost Bliss there are seven rows of railings, seven rows of nets, and seven rows of trees, all made of the four jewels and surrounding it on all sides. Therefore that land is called the Land of Utmost Bliss.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in four. First, the explanation of the railings.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Lan' is a railing. The horizontal is called 'lan,' and the vertical called 'shun.' It adorns the jeweled trees and surrounds the clusters of flowers.

blocks.text: Next, the explanation of the nets.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The nets': jeweled nets spread over, their light and color shining, hung all around, adorning and decking.

blocks.text: Third, the explanation of the rows of trees.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The rows of trees': the Contemplation Sutra says, 'Each tree is eight thousand yojanas high, complete in the flowers and leaves of the seven jewels.'

blocks.text: Fourth, the explanation of the four jewels.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The four jewels' are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

[Sub-commentary] Speaking generally, in the Land of Bliss, upon the jeweled ground, before each precious jewel and each pavilion-lodge, arrays of jeweled trees are set; around the jeweled trees are railings; and over the jeweled trees and railings are nets spread. Each in the number of seven rows is to symbolize the thirty-seven aids to bodhi. But whether tree, railing, or net, all are of the four jewels, to symbolize the seven factors of awakening not being apart from the four truths. In the Sahā world, the households of kings and ministers are not without this adornment; yet of the trees, it is but a thicket; of the railings, but wood and stone; of the nets, but silk and hemp; of the ground, but earth and rock; and of the cause, but human labor. Though the gods likewise have these, it is not like the Pure Land's proclaiming the Dharma-sound. The difference between the Pure Land and the impure land, and the difference in what is naturally made—is there no reason for it? The explanation cites the Contemplation Sutra: each tree is eight thousand yojanas high, complete in the flowers and leaves of the seven jewels. By this analogy, the adorned things go beyond the four jewels, as is also to be known. Now I should give in full the Larger Sutra and the Contemplation Sutra, setting each forth completely. It is not that I delight in verbosity; it is also to aid the faith and joy of those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land. The Contemplation Sutra says: 'Contemplating the jeweled trees, contemplate each one, forming the thought of rows of seven-jewel trees. Each tree is eight thousand yojanas high. These jeweled trees, complete in the flowers and leaves of the seven jewels, each flower and leaf in the color of a different jewel: from the lapis-lazuli color issues golden light, from the crystal color red light, from the agate color the light of conch-shell, from the conch-shell color the light of green pearls; coral and amber and all the jewels serve as reflection and adornment. A wonderful pearl-net covers the trees; on each tree there are seven rows of nets, and within each row of nets are five hundred ko?i of wonderful flower-palaces, like the palace of the Brahma-king, with heavenly youths naturally within. Each youth has five hundred ko?i of the Śākyamuni-vidruma jewels as necklaces, whose jewel-light shines a hundred yojanas, like the combining of a hundred ko?i of suns and moons, which cannot be fully named; the many jewels are inter-sprinkled, and within the colors it is highest. These jeweled trees, row matching row, leaf following leaf; among the leaves grow the wonderful flowers, upon which naturally are the seven-jewel fruits. Each leaf is twenty-five yojanas square, with a thousand colors and a hundred kinds of patterns, like heavenly necklaces; the many wonderful flowers are the color of Jambunada gold, like a wheel of fire turning about among the leaves; the many fruits spring up, like the vase of Shakra, with great light that transforms into banners, canopies, and jewel-covers. Within these jewel-covers are revealed all the Buddha-matters of the three thousand great-thousand worlds; the Buddha-lands of the ten directions also appear within them.' Again the Larger Sutra says: 'And there are seven kinds of jeweled trees. The single-jewel tree has root, trunk, branch, leaf, flower, and fruit all of one jewel. The two-jewel tree has them alternating with two jewels. The three-jewel, four-jewel, five-jewel, six-jewel, and seven-jewel trees are likewise; only the seven-jewel tree adds one more jewel at its nodes. These trees, each different, row against row, trunk against trunk, branch against branch, leaf facing leaf, flower following flower, fruit matching fruit—in rows hundreds and thousands deep, alternating with jeweled pools, and so on throughout the whole world. The glory and the light cannot be fully beheld.'

inline.s: Moreover, Shariputra, in the Land of Utmost Bliss there are pools of the seven jewels, filled with the water of the eight virtues. The bottom of the pools is wholly covered with golden sand. On the four sides the stairways and paths are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Above, there are pavilions and towers, also adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, conch-shell, red pearls, and agate. In the pools are lotus-flowers as large as carriage-wheels: the blue ones shine blue light, the yellow yellow light, the red red light, the white white light, subtle, wonderful, fragrant, and pure.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in six. First, the explanation of the pools of the seven jewels.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The pools of the seven jewels': the Contemplation Sutra says, 'Each pool's water is formed of the seven jewels; those jewels are soft, born of the wish-fulfilling jewel-king.'

[Sub-commentary] 'The pools of the seven jewels' are named from the water; hence it cites the Contemplation Sutra's pool-water as formed of the seven jewels to explain. Yet in the Sahā world, is there no water? It is born of the celestial one, so its substance is not of the seven jewels. Are there no jewels? They are born of the earth element, so their substance is not soft. The Pure Land's water is soft yet not yin, jewel yet not hard; this is why the pure and the impure differ. Not only this—that sutra also says: 'Its wish-fulfilling water flows among the flowers, going up and down along the trees.' Precisely because its substance is not of the celestial one, it can not only descend but also ascend; this is where the coarse and the fine are divided. Not only this—that sutra says: 'Its sound is subtle, preaching suffering and emptiness, impermanence and no-self, and the perfections; again there is praise of the Buddhas' marks and excellences. From the wish-fulfilling jewel-king springs golden, subtle, wonderful light, whose light transforms into birds of a hundred jewel-colors, singing in harmony and sweet melody, ever praising the thought of the Buddha, the thought of the Dharma, and the thought of the Sangha.' Precisely because its substance is of the mind alone, the insentient preaches the Dharma—this is where suffering and joy are distinguished.

blocks.text: Next, the explanation of the water of the eight virtues.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The eight virtues': the Tang translation says, first, clear and pure; second, cool; third, sweet and fine; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moistening; sixth, peaceful and harmonious; seventh, removing hunger and thirst; eighth, nourishing the various faculties.

[Sub-commentary] This differs slightly from what the Contemplation Sutra lists. It says: light, clear and cool, soft, fine, not foul; at the time of drinking it is suited, and after drinking there is no harm. The commentary again pairs the eight virtues with the five sense-entrances: pure is the form-entrance; not foul is the smell-entrance; light, cold, and soft are the touch-entrance; fine is the taste-entrance; suited and harmless is the dharma-entrance. The Miaozong Chao says: 'The commentary explains the eight virtues and pairs them with the five entrances; adding the preaching of the Dharma, that is the sound-entrance. Though they form six entrances, they are all wonderful realms; hence they cause the practitioner to quickly realize non-birth.' Also the Larger Sutra says: 'The water of the eight virtues, still and full, pure and fragrant, tasting like nectar. Those bodhisattvas, shravakas, and superior good people, when in the pools of the seven jewels bathe and wash their forms, if they wish the water to reach the foot, it reaches the foot; if the knee, to the knee; if the waist, the armpit, up to the neck, the water is likewise. If they wish it to pour over the body, all as they wish. If they wish the water to be as at first, it is at first. Warmth and coolness, all suited. It opens the spirit and releases the body, washing away feelings and thoughts; clear and bright, limpid, polished as if without form.'

blocks.text: Third, the explanation of the golden sand covering the ground.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The golden sand covering the ground': the Contemplation Sutra says, 'Gold forms the channels, and beneath the channels all the variously-colored vajra forms the bottom sand.'

[Sub-commentary] This sutra says only 'golden sand covering the ground,' while the Contemplation Sutra says 'vajra as the bottom sand.' Its text is brief. To speak fully, it should be as the Larger Sutra says: 'A gold pool has a bottom of silver sand; a crystal pool a bottom of lapis-lazuli sand; a coral pool a bottom of amber sand. A pool made of two jewels likewise has a bottom of two jewels. A gold and silver pool has for its bottom sand coral and amber; a coral and amber pool has bottom sand of conch-shell and agate. If three, four, and up to seven jewels form one pool, the bottom sand is likewise.' These jeweled pools, some forty li square, some fifty, some sixty, and so on progressively larger, up to twenty-four thousand four hundred eighty li square, like the great sea. These pools are where the bodhisattvas, the shravakas, and the superior good people grow; sometimes they bathe among them. As for that Buddha's pool, its size is twice this, formed of the seven jewels inter-sprinkled, with white-moon pearls, bright-moon pearls, and wish-fulfilling jewels as its bottom sand.

blocks.text: Fourth, the explanation of the four jewels.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Lapis lazuli' here means 'not far': it is not far from the city of Varanasi, and having this jewel it is so named. 'Crystal' here means 'water-jade.'

[Sub-commentary] 'Lapis lazuli' is Sanskrit, fully 'vaidurya,' meaning 'not far.' Hence the earlier form of the characters was 'liu-li'; being Sanskrit, later people, seeing it as a jade-kind, changed it to the current form. 'Crystal' is likewise Sanskrit, fully 'sphatika,' whose appearance is like this land's rock-crystal, having red, white, and blue colors. The characters should likewise follow, but people, seeing it like jade, changed them to the current form. 'Conch-shell' is Sanskrit, fully 'mukti-jalabha,' meaning 'a blue-white jewel.' The Great Commentary says: a great shell like the rim of a great carriage-wheel, and the rim is the wheel's rim. 'Red pearls': the Buddhabhumi Sastra says they come from a red worm; the Great Wisdom Treatise says the true pearls come from the belly of a fish, from bamboo, and from the brain of a snake—not necessarily born only in the oyster. 'Agate' is the Sanskrit translated 'agate jewel-color, like the brain of a horse,' hence the name. The characters formerly were 'ma-nao'; later people changed them to the jade-stone radicals.

blocks.text: Fifth, the explanation of the pavilions and towers.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The pavilions and towers': the Contemplation Sutra says, 'In the land of many jewels, upon each realm there are fifty ko?i of jeweled towers.' The Larger Sutra says: 'Its lecture-halls and pure abodes, palaces, towers, and pavilions, all adorned with the seven jewels and formed of themselves; and again with true pearls, bright-moon and wish-fulfilling jewels interwoven and covering over them.'

[Sub-commentary] The Larger Sutra also says: 'The Amitābha Buddha's lecture-halls and pure abodes are all formed of the natural seven jewels inter-sprinkled; and again with the seven jewels as pavilions, towers, and railings; again with the seven jewels as necklaces hanging and adorning the sides; again with white pearls, bright-moon pearls, and wish-fulfilling jewels interwoven, covering over all. They are supremely excellent and beautiful, pure and luminous, beyond all praise. The other palaces where the bodhisattvas and shravakas dwell are likewise. The palaces and towers where those gods and the world's people dwell, suited to their form, color, height, and size, whether of one jewel, two jewels, or even immeasurable many jewels, all are transformed and formed.'

blocks.text: Sixth, the explanation of the four flowers.

inline.s: [Commentary] Lingzhi says: 'The size of a carriage-wheel is hard to fix as a standard.' The Treatise on the Ten Abodes says: 'A wheel-king's thousand-spoke wheel has a circumference of fifteen li.' Below the four colors: the Contemplation Sutra says, 'In each pool there are six ko?i of seven-jewel lotus-flowers'—then it is not just four colors. Each lotus is round and equal, twelve yojanas—not merely the size of a carriage-wheel. The Larger Sutra says: 'The lotuses in the pools are sometimes one yojana'—from which one knows they reach a hundred thousand yojanas. Hence one knows that what is seen according to capacity differs as superior and inferior.

[Sub-commentary] 'The lotuses of the jeweled pools': one use is as the adornment within the Pure Land, and another is as the place of entrusting birth for those who practice Buddha-recitation. Because the beings of the Land of Bliss have no sexual desire, there are no male and female; having no male and female, there are no parents; having no parents, there is no womb-birth. Since there is no womb-birth, how could there be egg-birth or damp-birth? They should all be of metamorphic birth. Yet the Land of Bliss now discussed is the horizontal exit from the three realms, level with the Sahā world; wherefore those reborn there have the metamorphic as primary, though the three senses seem to be combined, because they entrust their substance to the lotus calyx while the flower dwells on the water. Hence the Larger Sutra says: 'The gods, humans, and even the flying and crawling creatures of the measureless worlds in the ten directions who are reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha are all metamorphically born in the lotus-flowers of the pools of the seven jewels. They naturally grow large, none of them suckled; they all eat the natural food. Their appearance and form, upright and pure, are not to be compared with worldlings, nor with gods and humans; they all receive the naturally pure-vacuous body and the immeasurable life.' Yet this may be said for the lower eight grades. If one is born in the highest grade, riding the vajra-platform, on arrival he immediately sees the Buddha, without passing through the lotus-birth, and at once realizes non-birth—this indeed has its reason. The explanation's 'what is seen according to capacity differs as superior and inferior' also follows from this.

inline.s: Shariputra, the Land of Utmost Bliss accomplishes such meritorious adornments.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two. First, the proper explanation of the scripture-text.

inline.s: [Commentary] The adornments of the land's boundaries are all accomplished by Amitābha's long-eon cultivation and the practice-vows of bodhi.

[Sub-commentary] As explained above, the various adornments are all adorned by Amitābha's merit. 'Merit' means power, and 'virtue' means function. These are all the great functions of liberation on the Tathagata's fruit, through which he receives and gathers living beings. Tracing far back to their cause: it was the forty-eight vows first issued from his initial mind, vowing to take the Land of Bliss; thereafter through immeasurable kalpas of cultivation he filled the vows; when the practice was complete the vows were accomplished, and when the vows were accomplished the land was pure.

blocks.text: Next, pointing to the cited texts.

inline.s: [Commentary] What the citation says: the Larger Sutra is the two-fascicle Sutra of Immeasurable Life, which speaks broadly of the Pure Land; the Contemplation Sutra is the sixteen-contemplation sutra, which broadly explains the practice-form. This sutra speaks briefly and is called in the world the Smaller Sutra, so named in contrast to the Larger Sutra.
