inline.s: Moreover, Shariputra, in that Buddha's land heavenly music is always played, the ground is of gold, and in the six periods of day and night there rains down the mandarava flowers. The beings of that land, always in the clear morning, each with their garment-hem gather the multitudes of wonderful flowers and go to offer them to the hundred thousand ko?i of Buddhas in the other directions; at the time of the meal they return to their own land, eat, and practice walking. Shariputra, the Land of Utmost Bliss accomplishes such meritorious adornments.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in six. First, the explanation of the heavenly music.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The heavenly music': the Contemplation Sutra says, 'The immeasurable gods perform heavenly music; and again there are instruments hanging in empty space, like heavenly jewel-banners, sounding of themselves without being struck.' The Larger Sutra says: 'There are also ten thousand natural kinds of music; and again the music-sounds are none other than Dharma-sounds, clear and floating, plaintive and bright, subtle and harmonious, which no other sound can equal.'

[Sub-commentary] 'Which no other sound can equal': the Larger Sutra says, 'As the world's emperor has ten thousand kinds of music, yet not one note of it equals a single note of the music of the wheel-turning sage-king, by a hundred, thousand, ten-thousand times. As the wheel-turning sage-king's ten thousand kinds of music do not equal a single note of the music of the Lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven, by a hundred, thousand, ten-thousand times. As the Trayastrimsa lord's ten thousand kinds of music do not equal a single note of the music of the sixth-heaven lord, by a hundred, thousand, ten-thousand times. As the sixth-heaven lord's ten thousand kinds of music do not equal a single note of the music of the seven-jewel trees in the land of Amitābha Buddha, by a hundred, thousand, ten-thousand times. And there are again the natural, various wonderful music whose sounds are none other than the wonderful Dharma, clear and floating, sweet and harmonious, foremost among all the sounds of the ten directions.'

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of gold as the ground.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Gold as the ground': the Contemplation Sutra says, 'Upon the lapis-lazuli ground, with golden cords interspersed and alternating, together with the seven jewels, marking its boundaries.' Now saying 'gold' is merely the adornment of the ground's surface.

[Sub-commentary] This smaller sutra is brief. If broadly explained, it is as the Larger Sutra says: 'In the land of Amitābha Buddha there are all the natural seven jewels—gold, silver, white silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and conch-shell—whose substance is gentle. With these seven jewels inter-sprinkled, the ground is formed; or with a single jewel alone as the ground. The light and color shine, wonderful and pure, transcending all the worlds of the ten directions. That land is expansive and vast, without limit; the ground is all level and right, with no Mount Sumeru and no vajra iron-ring, no various mountains, no great seas or small seas, no pits, wells, or valleys, and no dark places.'

blocks.text: Third, the explanation of the mandarava flowers.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Mandarava' here means 'white flower' and also 'agreeable to the mind.' But that land's light shines always, without relying on sun or moon, so there is no day and night. According to the Larger Sutra, the opening of the flowers and the songs of the birds mark the dawn, and the closing of the lotuses and the roosting of the birds mark the night. Again there are no four seasons—spring, autumn, winter, summer; never cold, never hot, always harmonious and suited.

[Sub-commentary] 'White flower, agreeable to the mind' is a brief raising of one of the four flowers. Fully it should be as the Lotus: 'The heavens rain four flowers: first, mandarava, this the small white flower; second, mahamandarava, the great white flower; manjushaka, the small red flower; mahamanjushaka, the great red flower.' The Larger Sutra also says: 'There are the heavenly utpala flowers, the padma flowers, the kumuda flowers, and the pundarika flowers—all heavenly flowers.' Because that Buddha's land, in its lords and attendants, in its proper and dependent, all have light, there is no sun, moon, yin and yang, no cold and heat, no four seasons. Yet to take the opening of the flowers and the songs of the birds as dawn, and the closing of the lotuses and the roosting of the birds as night—I privately fear this is still the flavor of the cohabitation Pure Land of ordinary and sage, in the interval between having and not yet having forgotten the impure land, because those reborn there are for the most part those who go with karma. If it be the upper three lands, there is no such appearance.

blocks.text: Fourth, the explanation of the garment-hem.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The garment-hem' is the lapel of the garment.

[Sub-commentary] Paramartha says: 'It is a foreign vessel for holding flowers.' The explanation retains two readings; the first is correct. For the hem is originally the lapel of the garment. When the heavenly flowers rain, why need one seek a vessel? One simply gathers them in the garment-hem, and from the lapel picks up the flowers and scatters them; having scattered, one lets down the lapel and forgets them. This is among the most agreeable matters in the Pure Land.

blocks.text: Fifth, the explanation of the offering.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Offering to a hundred thousand ko?i of Buddhas': the Larger Sutra says, 'Bearing the Buddha's power, in the space of one meal they go to the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and respectfully offer to the Buddhas.'

[Sub-commentary] This is still an abbreviated text. If given in full, the sutra says: 'The bodhisattvas in the land of Amitābha Buddha, bearing the Buddha's awesome power, in the space of one meal go to all the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and offer to the Buddhas. As their minds desire, flowers, incense, music, garments, canopies, banners, and countless offerings appear of themselves before them, precious, wonderful, and extraordinary, beyond all that the world has; they present them to the Buddhas and to the assemblies of the bodhisattvas and shravakas. Or if they wish to offer flowers, then in the air they are transformed into flower-canopies. The small ones are forty li in circumference, or fifty, or sixty, and so on progressively larger up to six hundred thousand li; each, following its size, stays in the air to form a round image, all facing downward, to complete the offering. The light and color shine, and the fragrance pervades, beyond all praise. Having been used, according to their order, they disappear in turn. The bodhisattvas, again in the air, together play the heavenly music, and with subtle sounds sing and praise the Buddha's virtues; they hear and receive the sutra-Dharma with measureless joy. Having offered, they suddenly rise lightly and return to their own land, still before the time of the meal.'

blocks.text: Sixth, the explanation of the time of the meal.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The time of the meal' is before noon. The Larger Sutra says: 'When one wishes to eat, bowls of the seven jewels appear of themselves before one, and the hundred flavors of food are of themselves full. Seeing the color and smelling the fragrance, one is naturally satisfied; body and mind are soft, with no attachment to flavor. Having eaten, it dissolves away; when the time comes, it appears again.'

[Sub-commentary] The Larger Sutra fully says: 'At the time of their meal, some wish for silver bowls, some for gold, some for lapis-lazuli and crystal bowls, some for coral, amber, conch-shell, and agate bowls; or they wish for bright-moon pearl, wish-fulfilling pearl, white jade, purple gold, and other bowls—all appear before them following their minds. The hundred flavors of food fill them, sour, salty, pungent, and bland, each as desired; plentiful without surplus, scanty without lack. Nor do they eat beyond measure because of its delicacy; they only use it to nourish their strength. Having eaten, it naturally dissolves without residue. Or merely seeing the color and smelling the fragrance, they think of it as food, and are naturally full and at ease, with no attachment to flavor; body and mind are clear and swift. Having used it, it naturally dissolves away; when they wish to eat again, it appears again as before. In that land, pure and serene, subtle and blissful, next to the unconditioned, the way of nirvāṇa.'

blocks.text: Fourth, the spiritual birds proclaiming the Dharma, in two. First, the reminder of the section.
Fourth, the spiritual birds proclaiming the Dharma.
Second, the explanation of the scripture, in two. First, the reminder of the section.

inline.s: Furthermore, Shariputra, in that land there are always birds of various kinds, wonderful and of many colors: white cranes, peacocks, parrots, shari birds, kalavinka birds, and the shared-life birds with two heads. These many birds, in the six periods of day and night, utter harmonious and elegant sounds. Their sounds proclaim and flow forth the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of bodhi, the eight limbs of the holy path, and such dharmas as these. When the beings of that land hear these sounds, they all give rise to the thought of the Buddha, the thought of the Dharma, and the thought of the Sangha.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in five. First, the explanation of 'wonderful.'

inline.s: [Commentary] The precious birds of the Pure Land differ from the feathered tribes of the Sahā, hence they are called 'wonderful.' The Tathagata spoke following the world, and the translator, taking their kinds, translated them.

[Sub-commentary] The feathered tribes of the Sahā, though they have precious birds, are not the transformation of light but verily born of karmic offense—how could they be called wonderful? Someone may doubt: since they are not of karmic offense, why do they have the same names? Hence the explanation: the Tathagata spoke following the world, so the translator, taking their kinds, translated; in truth they cannot be compared with those of this land.

blocks.text: Next, the separate explanation of the various birds.

inline.s: [Commentary] The three, the white crane and the rest, can be understood. 'Shari' here means the spring oriole, or the heron. 'Kalavinka' here means 'wonderful sound': while still in the shell, its sound already surpasses the other birds. The shared-life birds have two heads on one body, with the retribution the same but the consciousness different; what the Lotus calls 'jivamjivaka' is this.

[Sub-commentary] The rest are as explained in the text. As for the wonderful-sound bird, the character for shell should properly be 'kou,' and writing it as 'gun' is wrong. The Great Treatise says: 'The kalavinka in the shell has a sound surpassing the other birds'—this is it. The kalavinka and the shared-life bird, these two birds are not found in the eastern regions.

blocks.text: Third, the explanation of 'harmonious and elegant.'

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Harmonious and elegant' means the sound delights people; 'proclaiming and flowing forth' means the Dharma is spoken without obstruction.

[Sub-commentary] Though the sound delights people, it does not bewilder the ear or draw the mind; since the Dharma is spoken without obstruction, it can give rise to wisdom, reflection, and practice. That beings are all non-retrogressing is because of this.

blocks.text: Fourth, the explanation of the practice-grades, in two. First, the proper explanation of the four. First, the five faculties.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The five faculties': first, faith; second, diligence; third, mindfulness; fourth, concentration; fifth, wisdom. Able to give birth to the holy path, they are called faculties.

[Sub-commentary] The thirty-seven aids to bodhi, like a tree: first, taking the hearing of the Dharma as the seed, and reflection and practice as the watering; that is, the four abodes of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of supernormal power—these three, each not losing its season, with the causes and conditions accomplished, can give birth to the five faculties. When the faculties have gained power, they can push through the thick earth's five hindrances and spread the branches and leaves of the seven factors of bodhi, to bear the flowers and fruit of the right concentration of the eight-fold path; from the Sahā they make a great tree of coolness. Hence the Explanation of the Sequence of the Dharma-realm, first gate, says: 'First, the faculty of faith: faith in the right path and in the aiding dharmas can give birth to all outflow-free meditations and liberations; this is called the faculty of faith. Second, the faculty of diligence: having believed the right contemplation of the four abodes of mindfulness and the various aiding good dharmas, one redoubles effort, tirelessly seeking; this is called the faculty of diligence. Third, the faculty of mindfulness: thinking only of the right path and the aiding dharmas, with single-minded contemplation, not letting the evil and false enter; this is called the faculty of mindfulness. Fourth, the faculty of concentration: gathering the mind on the right path and the aiding dharmas, single-minded and still, corresponding and not scattered; this is called the faculty of concentration. Fifth, the faculty of wisdom: the wisdom of the four abodes of mindfulness, held by the concentration-dharma, the inner nature itself illumining, not known from another; this is called the faculty of wisdom.'

blocks.text: Next, the explanation of the five powers.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The five powers' have the same names as the faculties above; able to repel the karmic hindrances, they are called powers.

[Sub-commentary] First, the power of faith: faith in the right path and in the aiding dharmas; when the faculty of faith grows, it can ward off the various afflictions and is not moved by the various one-sided and lesser doubts; hence called the power of faith. Second, the power of diligence: when practicing this right path and the aiding dharmas, if the faculty of diligence grows, it can destroy the various laxities and indulgences and bring all the right and aiding dharmas to completion; this is the power of diligence. Third, the power of mindfulness: when thinking of this right path and the aiding dharmas, if the faculty of mindfulness grows, it can destroy the various false thoughts and accomplish the merits of right mindfulness that transcend the world; this is the power of mindfulness. Fourth, the power of concentration: when gathering the mind on the right path and the aiding dharmas, if the faculty of concentration grows, it can destroy the various scattered thoughts and put forth the various meditations of matters and principle; this is the power of concentration. Fifth, the power of wisdom: the wisdom of the four abodes of mindfulness, illumining and understanding all dharmas; if the faculty of wisdom grows, it can remove the various attachments of the false and the evil, and destroy the various one-sided and lesser wisdoms; hence called the power of wisdom.

blocks.text: Third, the seven factors of bodhi.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Bodhi' here means 'the factor of awakening,' or a branch. First, the awakening of mindfulness; second, the awakening of dharma-investigation; third, the awakening of diligence; fourth, the awakening of joy; fifth, the awakening of ease; sixth, the awakening of concentration; seventh, the awakening of equanimity.

[Sub-commentary] First, the awakening of mindfulness: mindfulness means reflection; when cultivating the various dharmas, one well knows, always keeping concentration and wisdom in balance. If the mind is drowsy, one should think to use the three factors of dharma-investigation, diligence, and joy, observing the dharmas, so as not to be drowsy. If the mind is restless, one should think to use the factor of removal, removing the faults of body and mouth; or use the factor of equanimity, letting go the contemplative wisdom; or use the factor of concentration, entering the right meditative concentration, gathering the scattered mind so that it does not move; this is called the factor of awakening. Second, the awakening of dharma-investigation: investigation means discrimination; when using wisdom to observe the dharmas, one can well distinguish the true and the false without mistakenly taking the false; hence the factor of dharma-investigation. Third, the awakening of diligence: unmixed is called pure, unbroken is called advance; when cultivating the dharmas, one well knows, not practicing useless asceticism, and in the various right dharmas ever able to use the mind single-mindedly without interruption; hence the factor of diligence. Fourth, the awakening of joy: joy means delight; when the mind accords with and realizes the true Dharma, upon attaining joy one well knows that this joy is not born from inverted dharmas, and abides in the true Dharma-joy; hence the factor of joy. Fifth, the awakening of ease, also called the factor of removal: removal means cutting off; when cutting off the various views and afflictions, one well knows, removing the false dharmas and increasing the true roots of goodness; hence the factor of removal. Sixth, the awakening of concentration: concentration means meditative concentration; when putting forth meditative concentration, one well knows the various concentrations and does not give rise to afflictions and false thoughts; this is called the factor of concentration. Seventh, the awakening of equanimity: leaving the realm to which views and thoughts are attached, one well knows it to be false and unreal and never recollects it again; hence the factor of equanimity.

blocks.text: Fourth, the eight limbs of the holy path.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'The eight limbs of the holy path,' which the sutras sometimes call the right eight-fold path: first, right view; second, right thought; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right diligence; seventh, right mindfulness; eighth, right concentration.

[Sub-commentary] Since these eight dharmas do not rely on the one-sided and the wrong in their practice, they are called right; and being able to lead to nirvāṇa, they are called path. First, right view: a person cultivating the outflow-free path sees the four truths clearly and breaks the various wrong views of non-Buddhists such as existence and non-existence; this is right view. Second, right thought: when a person sees the four truths, with right mindfulness he reflects, observes, and weighs, causing the contemplation to grow; this is right thought. Third, right speech: a person with outflow-free wisdom ever restrains the karma of speech, far from all false and untruthful words; this is right speech. Fourth, right action: a person with outflow-free wisdom cultivates and restrains his mind, abiding in pure right action, cutting off all wrong and false conduct; this is right action. Fifth, right livelihood: one who has left home ever leaves the five wrong kinds of livelihood and gain, and always lives by begging food; this is right livelihood. Sixth, right diligence: a person diligently cultivates the way of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, single-mindedly and with full attention without interruption; this is right diligence. Seventh, right mindfulness: a person thinks on the right path of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and the five ways of stilling the mind and the aiding dharmas, able to advance to nirvāṇa; this is right mindfulness. Eighth, right concentration: a person gathers the various scatterings, body and mind serene and still, rightly abiding in the principle of true emptiness, determined and unmoving; this is right concentration.

blocks.text: Second, pointing to the omissions.

inline.s: [Commentary] Of the thirty-seven aids, three groups are omitted—the four abodes of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of supernormal power—hence it says 'such dharmas.'

[Sub-commentary] Since the sutra omitted and abbreviated them, the explanation does not fill them in; but now I should fully set forth their meaning, as an aid to the reflection and practice of later students. The four abodes of mindfulness: mindfulness is the contemplation that observes, and the abode is the realm observed. The various beings, regarding the five aggregates of form, feeling, thought, activities, and consciousness, give rise to four inversions: regarding form they often give rise to the inversion of purity; regarding feeling, the inversion of joy; regarding thought and activities, the inversion of self; regarding consciousness, the inversion of permanence. To cause beings to cultivate these four contemplations to remove the four inversions, they are called the four abodes of mindfulness. First, contemplating the body as impure: the body has inner and outer; one's own body is the inner body, and the body of others is the outer body. These inner and outer bodies are all formed by gathering the parents' remains. From head to foot, contemplating each, it is wholly filth. Beings, inverted, hold it as pure and give rise to attachment; hence they are caused to contemplate the body as impure. Second, contemplating feelings as suffering: the reception of objects is called feeling; there is inner feeling and outer feeling—the feeling of the mind-faculty is inner feeling, and the feeling of the five faculties is outer feeling. Each faculty has agreeable feeling, disagreeable feeling, and neither-agreeable-nor-disagreeable feeling. Toward agreeable objects one gives rise to pleasurable feeling; toward disagreeable objects, painful feeling; toward neither-agreeable-nor-disagreeable objects, neutral feeling. Pleasurable feeling is the suffering of destruction; painful feeling is the suffering of suffering; neutral feeling is the suffering of activity. Beings, inverted, take suffering as joy; hence they are caused to contemplate feelings as suffering. Third, contemplating the mind as impermanent: the mind is the sixth consciousness. This consciousness-mind's nature is flowing; whether coarse or fine, inner or outer, thought after thought arises and perishes, all impermanent. Fourth, contemplating dharmas as selfless: dharmas have the good and the evil; people all, following dharmas, impute a self, saying that I can do good and I can do evil. Within good and evil dharmas there is originally no self. If the good dharma were the self, the evil dharma should be selfless; if the evil dharma were the self, the good dharma should be selfless. Beings, inverted, falsely impute a self; hence they are caused to contemplate dharmas as selfless. The four right efforts: first, evils already arisen, cause them to be forever cut off: the five hindrances and such afflictions cover the mind and separate it from the five roots of goodness; hence with single-minded diligence, by means of expedients, one cuts them off so they do not arise again. Second, evils not yet arisen, cause them not to arise: the five hindrances and such evil dharmas, though not yet arisen, if they later arise can block the five roots of goodness; hence with single-minded diligence, by expedients one cultivates so that they never arise. Third, good already arisen, cause it to grow: the five roots of goodness and such good dharmas, though already arisen, should be guarded and made to grow; hence with single-minded diligence, by expedients one cultivates so that they do not regress or perish. Fourth, good not yet arisen, cause it to arise: the five roots of goodness, though not yet arisen, for the sake of their arising, with single-minded diligence, by expedients one cultivates so that they arise. The four bases of supernormal power: first, the desire base: desire means aspiration and longing, taking delight in adorning that dharma; hence called desire. All dharmas one cultivates, if there is no delighting mind, the matter will not be accomplished; if one delights, the wish is attained; this is the desire base. Second, the mindfulness base: mindfulness means focusing the mind on that realm, single-mindedly abiding; hence called mindfulness. If one is not single-minded, the contemplation is cut off; if one can be single-minded, the wish is attained; this is the mindfulness base. Third, the diligence base: solely contemplating the principle, without intermingling; hence called diligence. All dharmas one cultivates, if there is no diligence, the matter will not be accomplished; if one can be diligent, the wish is attained; this is the diligence base. Fourth, the thought base: weighing and examining that realm; hence called thought. All dharmas one cultivates, if there is no thought, nothing is obtained and all is unaccomplished; if one can think, the wish is attained; this is the thought base.

blocks.text: Fifth, the explanation of the right mindfulness.

inline.s: [Commentary] Gushan says: 'The thought of the Buddha is like the king of physicians; the thought of the Dharma like a good physician; the thought of the Sangha like the one who tends the sick. With these three complete, the illness of affliction can be cured.' Again, contemplate your own mind: still yet ever illumining, the dharmas all brightly manifest, called the thought of the Buddha; illumining yet ever still, with no dharma to be obtained, called the thought of the Dharma; still-and-illumining non-dual, present yet gone, called the thought of the Sangha. This is the three jewels as one body.

[Sub-commentary] Gushan, in terms of two meanings, explains the three jewels: first, the distinct characteristics; second, the unified body. In the distinct characteristics he brings forth the object of thought; he does not speak of the characteristics of the three jewels. 'The king of physicians' and so on: the root of the illness of birth-and-death lies in affliction; if one wishes to cure it, without the Buddha, the great king of physicians, one cannot know the illness and recognize the medicine, nor give the medicine suited to the illness. Hence first the thought of the Buddha-jewel. However, though one has seen him, if one does not hear the Dharma to seek the prescription, and take it in combination, the illness will not be cured. Hence next the thought of the Dharma-jewel. Though one can rely on the Dharma to reflect and practice, if there is no good bodhisattva friend as fellow-practitioner, as a protecting support, to regulate one's food and show the taboos, the illness also will not be cured. Hence further the thought of the Sangha-jewel. If one wishes to know what is thought: one with the three bodies and the four wisdoms complete is the Buddha-jewel; what he spoke, the twelve divisions, is the Dharma-jewel; the bodhisattvas of the forty-one stations are the Sangha-jewel. After the Buddha's nirvāṇa there is again the enduring three jewels: casting gold and carving wood is the Buddha-jewel; the palm-leaves coming from the west is the Dharma-jewel; shaving the hair and dyeing the robes is the Sangha-jewel. If one can take refuge in and think on these two kinds, then the root of the illness of affliction can be cured, and the fruit of the illness of birth-and-death can be healed. Second, the unified body is what the text says: 'Again contemplate your own mind, still yet ever illumining' and so on. For Buddha means awakening, and awakening is illumination; hence by this mind's stillness but ever-illumination, with the dharmas brightly manifest, it is called the Buddha-jewel. Dharma means not-awakening, and not-awakening is stillness; hence by illumination but ever-still, with no dharma obtainable, it is called the Dharma-jewel. Sangha means harmony, and still-and-illumining non-dual is the meaning of harmony; hence by the still-and-illumining non-dual, present yet gone, it is called the Sangha-jewel.

blocks.text: Sixth, the explanation of the arising of the mind.

inline.s: [Commentary] Lingzhi says: 'In this world the mind is defiled and ever thinks of the five desires; in that land the mind is pure and single-mindedly thinks of the three jewels.' The rising and sinking of the two lands can be seen in this.

[Sub-commentary] As for the mind that arises in the face of objects, even Buddhas, sages, and worthies cannot be without it; one merely seeks its correctness. In the Sahā world the dusty objects are coarse and strong, so the mind that arises in the face of objects abides but is not right. In the Pure Land alone, what the ear hears is none other than the wonderful sound; so those who hear these sounds all give rise to the mind of deep thought of the three jewels. This is precisely what is called 'the mind arising yet not abiding, not abiding yet the mind arising.'

blocks.text: Second, resolving the doubt, in two. First, the reminder of the section.
Second, resolving the doubt.
Second, the explanation of the scripture, in two. First, setting forth the scripture.

inline.s: Shariputra, do not say that these birds are really born of karmic retribution. Why? In that Buddha's land there are no three evil paths. Shariputra, in that Buddha's land there is not even the name of an evil path, much less its reality. These many birds are all the transformations made by Amitābha Buddha, desiring to make the sound of the Dharma flow abroad.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two. First, the explanation that in the Pure Land the evil paths have a name but no substance.

inline.s: [Commentary] The birds and beasts of the turbid world are produced by karmic offense; how could the Pure Land have such? Hence it says 'do not say they are born of karmic retribution.' Therefore the Larger Sutra's fundamental vow of Dharmakara the bhiksu says: 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be in my land hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, may I not attain the right awakening.'
[Sub-commentary] 'The birds and beasts of the turbid world' below raises the doubt; 'hence it says' below resolves it; 'therefore the Larger Sutra' below cites the evidence.

blocks.text: Next, the explanation that in the Pure Land the evil paths have neither name nor substance.

inline.s: [Commentary] But that land is pure, and has not even the name of an evil path, much less the real substance born of karmic retribution. All these are the transformations made by that Buddha. Hence the Contemplation Sutra says: 'From the wish-fulfilling jewel-king springs golden, subtle, wonderful light, whose light transforms into birds of a hundred jewel-colors, singing in harmony and sweet melody, praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.' Lingzhi says: 'Know that these birds are precisely the Tathagata's supernormal power, desiring to make the sound of the Dharma flow freely; know that they are not born of karmic retribution.'
[Sub-commentary] 'But that land' below properly shows it has none; 'all are' below shows why it now has them. 'Hence the Contemplation Sutra' below cites the evidence; 'Lingzhi' below cites the same.

blocks.text: Fifth, the wind, the trees, and the music-sounds, in two. First, the reminder of the section.
Fifth, the wind, the trees, and the music-sounds.
Second, the explanation of the scripture, in two. First, setting forth the scripture.

inline.s: Shariputra, in that Buddha's land a gentle wind stirs the rows of jeweled trees and the jeweled nets, giving forth subtle sounds, like the simultaneous playing of a hundred thousand kinds of music; those who hear these sounds naturally give rise to the thought of the Buddha, the thought of the Dharma, and the thought of the Sangha. Shariputra, the Land of Utmost Bliss accomplishes such meritorious adornments.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two. First, citing the sutra by analogy to make clear.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Larger Sutra says: 'A gentle wind slowly stirs, blowing the jeweled trees, which bring forth immeasurable wonderful Dharma-sounds; these sounds flow abroad, pervading the Buddha-lands; those who hear them attain the dharma of deep patience.' The Contemplation Sutra again says: 'Its wish-fulfilling water flows among the flowers, preaching suffering and emptiness, impermanence and no-self, and the perfections.'

blocks.text: Next, citing another passage to make clear the purity.

inline.s: [Commentary] Gushan says: 'Though there are jeweled towers and golden pools as delight to the eye, they are not the sensual colors that bewilder; rather they enable one to reach the mind-only and the realm-less. Though there are the wind, the trees, and the birdsong as pleasure to the ear, they are not the seductive sounds that disturb; rather they enable one to think of the three jewels and to have a refuge.'

[Sub-commentary] Those in the world who detest disturbance will surely shut off sight and hearing from what is seen and heard, thus falling into the loss of lopsidedness. Those who delight in splendor will surely give themselves to ease amid sound and color, thus entangling in the toil of turmoil. In all cases, in the evil world of the five turbidities, both faculties and dust are impure. If one has neither the contemplation that realizes emptiness nor the gate that analyzes form, then whether advancing or retreating, who can escape fault? How much better the Pure Land: it lacks not the enjoyments of the jeweled towers and the golden pools, and joins to them the delight of wind, trees, and birdsong—seeing color without bewilderment, hearing sound without disturbance, without the toil of discrimination. And it enables one to reach that the realm is mind-only, to think deeply of the three jewels, without the loss of lopsidedness. The wonder of the Pure Land takes the middle way with composure. One who hears this and does not seek rebirth is not a worthy man.
